articles.title: Call for a transdiagnostic and ecologically valid assessment of youth psychopathology in daily life
articles.authors: Anja Christine Feneberg; Mitja D Back; Aleksandra Kaurin; David R. Kolar; Maximilian Monninger; Philip Samuel Santangelo; Tanja Hechler
articles.abstract:
Youth psychopathology is a pressing global challenge. High comorbidity rates and only moderate psychotherapy effects highlight the need for transdiagnostic approaches, which target mechanisms cutting across diagnostic categories to better understand the etiology and maintenance of mental disorders. Traditional diagnostic instruments, however, face limitations such as recall bias and inability to capture the dynamic, context-dependent nature of youth psychopathology. Recent advances in ecological momentary assessment (EMA) now enable real-time, naturalistic measurement, but EMA studies in youth rarely adopt a transdiagnostic focus, and transdiagnostic research has seldom incorporated EMA.
This paper is a call for the integration of transdiagnostic science and EMA methods to advance clinical research and practice in youth. Although guidelines exist for EMA design in youth, recommendations on how to realize a transdiagnostic perspective using EMA is currently lacking. We summarize recent developments primarily in the field of adult research and outline key steps for the development and evaluation of a transdiagnostic EMA tool for youth. We conclude our call by outlining implications for transdiagnostic EMA research, including the potential of bridging theoretical transdiagnostic models and clinical applications.

articles.title: Just the facts: How dialogues with AI reduce conspiracy beliefs
articles.authors: Thomas H Costello; Gordon Pennycook; David Gertler Rand
articles.abstract: Personalized dialogues with AI substantially reduce conspiracy beliefs. To identify why, we conducted two experiments with U.S. adults recruited online (total N = 2,193) that removed possible causes one at a time. The debunking effect was robust to disclosing the AI's persuasive goal, framing the exchange as a debate, instructing the AI to inform rather than persuade, halving its response length, altering how beliefs were measured, and replacing the dialogue with a single tailored message. Only instructing the AI to persuade without factual evidence and arguments substantially reduced the debunking effect. Content analyses of the AI's output and participants' own accounts linked larger reductions in conspiracy beliefs to factual argumentation rather than rapport, storytelling, or appeals to empathy. AI dialogues appear to reduce conspiracy beliefs primarily by supplying relevant, well-reasoned counterevidence. Our results suggest that humans might be similarly effective if they could supply comparable evidence.

articles.title: Psychology in 2125: A Developmental Science of Living Sense-Making
articles.authors: Peter J. Marshall
articles.abstract: A century from now, the computational framework at the center of psychology will no longer organize the discipline. As used here, "computational" names a broad information-processing ontology: meaning is specified in advance, rather than generated through the activity, history, and situation of living beings. This assumption fits engineered systems, but it misdescribes living ones. This article argues that three converging shifts are destabilizing that framework. The first undermines the computational account of inheritance: organisms develop through activity within configurations of constraints reconstituted across generations, not through the readout of genetic programs. The second displaces its account of psychological structure: psychological phenomena unfold as trajectories of coordination rather than as stable traits, with reliability and variability arising from the same generative process. The third sharpens the first two: artificial intelligence systems produce fluent performance without embodiment, developmental history, or any stake in the world. This contrast reveals what living organization contributes. The psychology implied by these shifts treats development as foundational, not as a subfield. It understands psychological constructs as patterns of activity that persons sustain over time, and is better positioned to address a century of changing human ecologies. This future psychology will be a developmental science of living sense-making.

articles.title: The Male Abstraction Bias in Internet Culture and Large Language Models
articles.authors: Douglas Guilbeault; Bhargav Srinivasa Desikan
articles.abstract: Conceptual abstraction and gender are two equally central aspects of the human mind, yet they have traditionally been studied in isolation from one another, as though they were fundamentally separate. Here, we find gender and abstraction are systematically linked throughout the space of concepts spanning single (N = 40,000) and multi-word expressions (N = 67,000): across billions of words and millions of images on the internet —  and across numerous measurement techniques, including human and AI classifications — more abstract concepts are more associated with men, a pattern we show replicates in languages around the world. This male abstraction bias not only holds across semantic domains, but it also maps onto grammatical structure: verbs and adverbs are more abstract and more male-coded, revealing a system-wide trace of stereotypes accentuating agentic qualities in men. Furthermore, we show this bias readily emerges in the free associations humans and AIs produce in controlled online tasks, indicating its psychological internalization and its algorithmic reproduction. These findings identify a latent structure in conceptual space that unifies a range of stereotypes: for example, framings of women as more embodied, emotional, and warm, versus men as more cognitive, rational, and competent; as well as erroneous views of men as better at mathematics, science, and engineering. More broadly, by analyzing an unprecedently large, multimodal sample of online data, we provide culture-wide evidence of gender as a core organizing principle shaping conceptual space far beyond the characterization of people and social roles.

articles.title: Indikationskatalog Musiktherapie in der neurologischen Rehabilitation
articles.authors: Monika Baumann; Stefan Mainka; Anna Badorrek; Silja Molle
articles.abstract: Der Indikationskatalog Musiktherapie in der neurologischen Rehabilitation gibt einen systematischen Überblick über die musiktherapeutische Praxis in diesem Bereich. Er verbindet wissenschaftliche Grundlagen und klinische Expertise, berücksichtigt den multidisziplinären Kontext und das spezifische Setting in der Neurorehabilitation und geht im Detail auf die Symptomatiken der Patient:innen ein. Der Katalog listet 5 Indikationsbereiche: Bewusstsein, Sensomotorik, Kommunikation, Kognition und Psyche. Für jeden Bereich werden in Tabellenform einzelnen Symptomen die jeweiligen Therapieziele und Interventionen zugeordnet. Das Spektrum der musiktherapeutischen Interventionen reicht von basalem Kontaktaufbau bei Menschen mit Bewusstseinsstörungen über funktionales Training bei motorischen, sprachlichen und kognitiven Beeinträchtigungen bis zur Behandlung psychischer Symptome. Dabei werden sowohl in anderen Fachbereichen übliche Methoden der aktiven und rezeptiven Musiktherapie aufgeführt als auch spezifische Methoden für die Arbeit mit neurologischen Patient:innen (einschließlich der neurologischen Musiktherapie®). So dient der Katalog gleichermaßen als Handlungsgrundlage für die musiktherapeutische Praxis als auch der Information benachbarter Disziplinen und der Kostenträger.

articles.title: Same-Emotion Synchrony During Laboratory-Based Intimate Partner Aggression
articles.authors: Wyatt Thomas Brown
articles.abstract: The moment-to-moment coupling of partners’ facial expressions (i.e., synchrony) is a core channel of nonverbal coordination, yet it has rarely been measured during overt conflict. Using recorded facial expressions during a laboratory-based intimate partner aggression task, I estimated trial-level, same-emotion expressive synchrony, decomposed from between-dyad similarity, for 51 dyads (N = 102 participants). Confirmatory analyses focused on emotional synchrony for anger, disgust, and happiness and tested whether a forced-break manipulation moderated synchrony. Happiness synchrony was robust. Anger synchrony was not detected. Disgust synchrony was not reliably distinguished from zero, though statistical power was limited. Contrary to the preregistered hypotheses, condition moderated only happiness synchrony, and in the opposite direction to what was anticipated. Positive coupling was stronger in the forced-break condition than the immediate-response condition, rather than remaining stable. Structured pauses during conflict may afford partners an opportunity to coordinate positive affect rather than serving only to interrupt negative affect. Altogether, partners’ positive emotional expressions during a laboratory-based intimate partner aggression task couple, and this coupling is sensitive to the structure of the interaction.

articles.title: A set of dynamical rules for conversational progression act as a precursor to collective cognition
articles.authors: Zachary P Rosen; Rick Dale
articles.abstract: Conversation unfolds between speakers as a series of coordinated updates from prior ideas expressed in earlier utterances to new sets of ideas. This process of speakers and conversation partners jointly updating prior "conversation states" is an important piece of the cognitive scaffolding that enables social coordination, and even collective cognition -- the capacity for individuals to pool their cognitive resources to solve problems together. However, a functional data-driven description of how this process works is missing in the extant literature. This report provides a functional description of how conversation states are updated in terms of information-theoretic processes, while analyzing a corpus of 5,448 conversations in nine typologically diverse languages. Our results show that individuals form a strongly connected distributed computational system during conversation, which generates new information according to a power-law distribution. These properties of conversation may be the foundation upon which human interaction encodes and solves a potentially unbounded number of problems and ideas.

articles.title: Puberty in autism: A window into emerging mental health risk
articles.authors: Giorgia Picci; Lucina Q. Uddin; Caitlin R. Mills; Holly A Feser Stessman
articles.abstract: Puberty is a period of major neural reorganization, accompanied by changing demands to navigate increasingly complex social environments and the emergence of many mental health disorders. Although pubertal processes are becoming well-documented in neurotypical youth, the field has only begun to interrogate these processes in youth with autism. In this mini-review, we evaluate evidence regarding altered pubertal development in autism based on studies examining physical development milestones and neuroendocrine axes pertinent to adrenarche and gonadarche. We review studies linking pubertal factors with mental health symptoms in autistic youth to assess potential puberty-related links to risk for co-morbid psychopathology. We bring together multiple literatures across human and animal models to assess evidence of consensus across fields. Findings suggest that aspects of puberty may be accelerated in autism, and that they may be at elevated risk for co-morbid mental health symptoms. We conclude with recommendations for future research, including the need for integration across pubertal, neural, and mental health measures to delineate how trajectories of risk may unfold in youth with autism.

articles.title: Auditing the measurement quality of societal progress:  A six-criterion framework applied to 99 indicators
articles.authors: Peter Diep; Cory J Clark; Molly Matthews; Phil Tetlock; Igor Grossmann
articles.abstract: Policymakers and researchers need societal indicators they can inspect, obtain data for, and trust to be up-to-date. We performed an audit of candidate measures of human progress, benchmarking 99 widely used indicators spanning domains critical to human welfare and societal change: civil liberties, climate, economy, education, peace and war, public health, technology, and well-being. We drew 62 indicators from expert nominations, augmented by 37 further commonly used indicators supplied by our research team. We audited these indicators against six basic criteria social scientists rely on as prerequisites for measurement validity: definability, quantifiability, public data availability, global population coverage, documentation, and temporal resolution. Only 32% of indicators (43% of those with public data) met all six criteria. Documentation and temporal resolution were the most common failures, and we found no reliable differences across domains. Our findings suggest that many areas of human progress and societal change rely on markers that often cannot be audited, raising questions about the empirical foundation of global policy initiatives, and pointing to ways to improve measurement of global progress.

articles.title: Emoticon variation: Eyes, mouths, and mirrorings are more meaningful than noses and rotations
articles.authors: Dominic Thompson; Shuping Ling
articles.abstract: Emoticons can visually differ in various minor ways. This includes presence or absence of an element, like the 'nose' or 'tear' in the :-) and :'( emoticons, differences in orientation, as in the :) versus (: emoticons, or a change to an element, such as the 'eyes' in the :) versus ;) emoticons. It is unclear which types of variation impact meaning, or whether the visual scale of variation predicts the degree of impact on meaning. We investigated emoticon use, contextual suitability, and perceived meaning equivalence across positive, negative, and sarcastic contexts. Given that emoticons can clarify message intent and may be used as a compensatory tool in a second-language, we also compared L1 (n = 151) and L2 (n = 119) users of English. Utilising emoticons that were produced by participants in earlier research, a series of ratings and selections revealed systematic differences in the effects of visual variations. Changes to the nose element and rotation had relatively little impact on perceived meaning, whereas mirroring and changes to the eyes or mouth had progressively greater effects, with mouth variation producing the greatest impact. L1 and L2 users patterned closely in overall usage, contextual suitability judgements, and interpretations of meaning equivalence. However, differences emerged for particular variants, especially interpretations of winking and tongue-out emoticons, as well as greater L2 use and acceptance of upright-oriented kaomoji. These findings suggest that aspects of emoticon meaning are systematically influenced by constituent elements, but are partly conventionalised within language communities, with implications for cross-linguistic digital communication and digital literacy.

articles.title: Same Gossip, Different Judgment: Why  Inappropriate Workplace Gossip Is More  Acceptable When It Targets AI
articles.authors: Clarissa Sabrina Arlinghaus; Lukas Kroner; Günter W. Maier
articles.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is rapidly becoming an active member of organizational teams. Yet successful human–AI symbiosis depends on more than intelligent algorithms, trust calibration, or effective task allocation. As AI becomes a social interaction partner, organizations must also establish shared moral norms governing how artificial teammates are treated. Surprisingly, little is known about whether employees apply the same ethical standards to AI coworkers as they do to human colleagues or why these judgments differ. 
To address this question, we conducted two preregistered online vignette experiments (N = 546) in which participants observed coworkers engaging in identical inappropriate workplace gossip directed either at a human colleague or an AI teammate. Building on Bandura's theory of moral disengagement, we tested whether cognitive moral disengagement explains differences in observers' moral evaluations and willingness to intervene. 
Across both studies, participants consistently judged gossip about an AI teammate as more morally acceptable and reported significantly lower willingness to intervene than when the same behavior targeted a human colleague. AI also increased endorsement of all eight mechanisms of moral disengagement. Parallel mediation analyses showed that moral disengagement fully accounted for the effects of target identity on both outcome variables, indicating that AI changes the cognitive processes through which observers evaluate unethical workplace behavior. Although the specific mechanisms contributing unique indirect effects varied somewhat across studies, dehumanization and distortion of consequences emerged as the most robust mediators. An exploratory analysis further demonstrated that these effects generalized across male and female perpetrators. 
These findings extend research on human–AI symbiosis by identifying shared moral norms as a previously overlooked prerequisite for successful collaboration. They suggest that organizations should focus not only on designing trustworthy AI systems but also on fostering ethical workplace cultures in which inappropriate behavior is evaluated according to the behavior itself rather than whether its target is human or artificial.

articles.title: Becoming Hybrid Selves:  Interacting with Artificial Minds and Bodies
articles.authors: Anna Ciaunica; Shaun Gallagher
articles.abstract: Humans have long tried to make artificial versions of our minds and bodies and other life forms. Recent technological advances are poised to open the Pandora box and explore whether these artificial agents will become more human or alive. In this paper we argue that this question needs to be addressed in tandem with the equally valid counterpart: to what extent do interactions with artificial others make humans less human and more artificial? Living systems such as human organisms are fundamentally open systems, continuously shaped and constituted by exchanges and interactions with the physical and social world. Thus, we suggest that we ourselves may become hybrid through our interactions with our artificial creations. Being surrounded by artificial agents from the cradle and across the lifespan may transform us, humans, into hybrid creatures. It is not only the passive and rapid absorption of the increasingly complex cognitive content that matters, nor the mere sophistication of the conversational exchanges with AI agents or embodied interactions with robots. Rather, the very nature of interaction itself matters too. It’s not what we learn, but how we learn and with whom we learn and what happens in between us and our creations.

articles.title: Promoting Honesty in Childhood: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis of Strategies to Reduce Cheating and Lying
articles.authors: MoZheng; Liyang Sai
articles.abstract: Honesty plays a vital role in children’s moral development, social trust, and cooperation, making it important to identify effective ways to promote honest behavior. Although numerous strategies have been tested, findings have varied considerably across studies. It therefore remains unclear which strategies reliably reduce dishonesty, which are comparatively more effective, and what accounts for this heterogeneity. We systematically reviewed 82 experimental studies involving 11,283 children and conducted separate network meta-analyses of cheating and lying. To clarify heterogeneity across diverse strategies, we organized them by their primary proximal target into social-influence, physical-context, and internal-standard activation approaches. Six strategies reduced cheating: promises, environmental nudges, negative moral stories, moral reputation, approval-based strategies, and self-awareness. Nine reduced lying: direct observational learning, moral emotions, combined strategies, approval-based strategies, positive moral stories, self-awareness, injunctive norms, promises, and positive descriptive norms. Promise and environmental nudges ranked highest for cheating, whereas direct observational learning and moral emotions ranked highest for lying. Among five strategies examined in both networks, promises, approval-based strategies, and self-awareness reduced both forms of dishonesty, and positive moral stories were less effective for cheating than for lying. In contrast, negative moral stories significantly reduced cheating but not lying. Moderator analyses found no robust moderators for cheating, but lying-reduction effects were weaker in Western than Eastern samples. Overall, these findings suggest that children’s honesty can be shaped by targeted psychological strategies, and offers an integrative basis for understanding and refining honesty-promotion strategies in childhood.

articles.title: German Adaptation and Psychometric Evaluation of the Conversation Questionnaire
articles.authors: Peter Bang; Lilly Fimpel; Joel Baisch; Victoria Pierz; Dirk Wildgruber; Yulia Oganian
articles.abstract:
Background: The Conversation Questionnaire (CQ) assesses everyday conversational difficulties through items developed with autistic adults. We translated the CQ into German and examined whether its psychometric properties reproduced the original findings.

Methods: Translation, author consultation, and cognitive debriefing with 15 self-reported autistic adults preceded validation in 185 native German-speaking adults. Participants reported an autism diagnosis (diagnosed), suspected or self-identified autism (suspected), or neither. We reanalyzed the original data (n = 266) to provide comparable benchmarks. We approximated the original broader cognitive-ability comparison with nonverbal matrix reasoning and extended validation to the recall of childhood coordination difficulties.

Results: Item response theory modeling closely reproduced two dimensions: difficulty knowing what to say (15 items) and misunderstandings or behaviors affecting conversation (21 items). Only two of 36 items showed shifted loadings, while reliability remained high for both dimensions (.94 and .90, respectively). As in the reanalyzed original data, both dimensions distinguished the diagnosed and neither groups. The suspected group had intermediate average scores, with overlapping individual scores across groups. Correlations with the CQ’s Core Language Difficulties and Negative Interaction Style control subscales were stronger for the second dimension, while correlations with reasoning performance were near zero. Extending the original validation, both dimensions correlated strongly with recalled childhood coordination difficulties (r = .64–.71).

Conclusion: These findings support the German CQ as a reliable, community-informed measure for characterizing conversational experiences among autistic and non-autistic German-speaking adults. Our findings also connect conversational experiences to childhood coordination abilities, showing the questionnaire’s relevance to broader neurodevelopmental research.

articles.title: When Does Reputation Help the Future? Audience Presence and Identity Disclosure in Intergenerational Resource Dilemmas
articles.authors: Mingyuan Sheng; Ye Niu; Xiaoli Ling
articles.abstract: Many environmental problems, from climate change to resource depletion, are intergenerational dilemmas: the present generation bears conservation costs, whereas the benefits go to future generations, who can neither observe nor reciprocate. Reputation reliably sustains cooperation among contemporaries, but whether it works across generations remains unclear. In two experiments using an intergenerational goods game, we examined how the audience of disclosure and the type of information disclosed affect contributions to a resource passed from one generation to the next, and whether social value orientation (SVO) moderates these effects. In Experiment 1, disclosing to the next generation what participants had contributed increased the rate of sustained generations but did not reliably increase individual contributions or narrow the gap between prosocial and proself individuals. In Experiment 2, disclosing the same information to present peers increased both individual contributions and the rate of sustained generations. Adding names and faces was tentatively associated with a further increase in contributions, although this condition was recruited in a separate wave. These gains came mainly from proself individuals, whose contributions no longer differed from those of prosocial individuals when names and faces were disclosed. The findings suggest that disclosure promotes intergenerational cooperation chiefly when it reaches an audience present at the time of decision, and that identifiability matters most for those least motivated to cooperate. Making conservation visible to future generations may not be enough; it may also need to be visible to someone now, suggesting a potentially low-cost approach to promoting environmental cooperation.

articles.title: Unlearning Modal Existential Constructions in L2 English: Implicational Universals and Frequency
articles.authors: Hunter Brakovec; Rex Sprouse
articles.abstract:
For many years, the problem of preemption has been discussed in second language acquisition research, i.e., how a learner ‘unlearns’ an initially transferred representation when the input does not provide contradictory evidence. In this study we examine how Yang’s (2002) Variational Learning model can account for cases of preemption. To do so, we address the expungement of Modal Existential Constructions (MECs) from the L2 English Interlanguage grammar of L1 Spanish and French learners. Using an acceptability 
judgement task, we analyze participants’ retreat from non-facilitative transfer considering two implicational universals associated with MECs and frequency effects. We find that the more marked an element is on an implicational hierarchy, the easier it is to remove. However, there is also evidence that frequency interacts with markedness to affect the rate of restructuring. These findings suggest a need to more seriously consider how domain-specific (language universals) and domain-general learning mechanisms (frequency) interact during second language acquisition and grammar restructuring.

articles.title: Red Tears. Blue Dreams: The Freudian Defense Mechanisms and Object Relations in Jimmy Alcantara’s Paired Narratives (Red ang Luha ni Michael and Blue ang Kobre Kama ni Jake)
articles.authors: Giancarlo Vincent Aguirre; Jerrymay S. Arroyo; Rinalyn B. Panganiban
articles.abstract: This study examines Jimmy Alcantara’s Red ang Luha ni Michael and Blue ang Kobrekama ni Jake through a psychoanalytic lens, focusing on the manifestation of denial, displacement, fantasy, and projection in thoughts, emotions, and behaviors of Ricky. Using a qualitative literary analysis through the literary lens of psychoanalytic approach, the study applies the Hierarchy of Defense Mechanisms and Defense Mechanism Rating Scales Q-Sort (DMRS-Q) framework of Di Giuseppe and Perry (2021) as the basis for identifying and interpreting defensive patterns in the narratives. Object Relations Theory serves as a complementary perspective in examining Ricky’s emotional attachment to Michael and the psychological significance of objects associated with their relationship. The findings reveal that Ricky employs denial in resisting threatening realities, displacement in redirecting emotional conflict toward objects and his surroundings, fantasy in constructing an idealized family through Jake, and projection in attributing his psychological conflict to Michael. The analysis further demonstrates that the scarlet paint, transformed apartment, blue bedspread, and Jake transcend their material functions and become symbolic extensions of Ricky’s emotional attachment and desire for intimacy, stability, and belonging. Altogether, the findings suggest that Alcantara portrays psychological conflict through the interaction of defensive processes and symbolic attachment, gradually blurring the boundary between Ricky’s internal desires and external reality. The study contributes to a psychoanalytic reading of contemporary Filipino literature by demonstrating how defense mechanisms and object relations can illuminate the representation of emotional dependency, attachment, and psychological fragmentation in literary narratives.

articles.title: Online Relationship Search: A Computerized Review from A Media-Market Perspective
articles.authors: Junwen M. Hu; Xiaoran Cui
articles.abstract: This scoping review surveys quantitative online dating research from a media-market perspective. We conceptualize online dating as online relationship search, which refers to two-sided matching activities that capitalize features of online dating platforms as both media and markets. Accordingly, we reviewed findings about the links between search strategies and outcomes, particularly covering a stream of strategies aimed to unleash the potential of online dating as media-markets: endorsing online dating as a venue for relationship search, expanding access to market options, optimizing matching procedures, and enhancing mutual understanding via interaction. A total of 134 studies were included via manual and computerized screening. First, pre-2010s research tended to find meeting a partner via an online dating site associated with higher relationship quality whereas post-2010s research often showed dating apps associated with less favorable search outcomes. Second, both excessive and inadequate access to options were found to be counterproductive. Third, meta-cognition about matching procedures were found to enhance matching outcomes. Fourth, daters were found to leverage different communication modalities/affordances for achieving different goals (garnering attention vs. facilitating long-term development). Findings suggest that successful searches can be facilitated by strategies that capitalize media market potential at different stages of search. We discuss how the media-market perspective may contribute to future work.

articles.title: Factors Associated with Meaning in Life Among Hispanic Adults in the Post-Pandemic  Period: A Cross-Sectional Study Across 16 Countries
articles.authors: Efrén Martínez; Orlando Scoppetta; Maria Juliana Montoya
articles.abstract:
This cross-sectional study examined post-pandemic levels of meaning in life and its 
associated factors among Hispanic adults (N = 10,142) aged 18 to 78 years old, residing 
across 16 countries. Analysis revealed that 50.2% of the participants experienced low levels 
of meaning in life. Controlling for fixed country effects, mental health, occupational purpose, 
gratitude, friendships, and engagement in meaningful activities emerged as variables 
associated with higher meaning in life. Conversely, low perceived workplace success, 
absence of gratitude, and heavy social media consumption were linked to lower meaning. 
Key sociodemographic markers, including income, education, and gender, showed no 
significant associations with meaning in life. This non-significance suggests that meaning in 
life functions as an accessible resource available to individuals regardless of their 
sociodemographic factors. These findings indicate that post-pandemic recovery across 
Hispanic populations must extend beyond economic indicators to prioritize accessible 
community-based mental health integration and social infrastructure, offering an evidencebased starting point for designing culturally grounded interventions to promote meaning in 
life.

articles.title: Effects of Self- and Other-Referencing Language on Engagement with Science Content on Social Media: A Field Experiment
articles.authors: Zuhe Liu; Joshua L. Schlichting; Lauren K Fink
articles.abstract: The present study tested whether the self-reference effect (SRE)—individuals’ tendency to engage with information related to themselves—can increase engagement with science content on social media. In a 12-week field experiment, we published 34 Instagram posts and 10 YouTube videos featuring a science lab’s activities. Captions and video titles were randomly assigned to either a self-referencing (SR) condition (using second-person pronouns), or an other-referencing (OR) condition (using third-person pronouns). Engagement was assessed using platform metrics such as likes and shares. Contrary to expectations, SR content did not yield higher engagement, whereas OR content yielded significantly higher shares. Exploratory analyses further indicated that OR content yielded higher composite engagement scores. These findings suggest that self-referencing language may have limited effectiveness for science communication in social media settings. Importantly, this study opens avenues for further research on how content framing strategies influences science content engagement on social media.

articles.title: Who Writes the Self? Identity Shift Persists Under AI-Assisted Writing
articles.authors: Zoë Natalia Cullen; Nicole Ellison; Jordyn Young; Andrea Forte
articles.abstract: Identity shift theory holds that selective online self-presentation can shift self-perception toward the portrayed identity, but its mechanisms assume that the presenter wrote the presentation. Generative AI now lets people publish self-presentations they did not fully compose. In a preregistered 2 (extraversion vs. introversion) × 3 (manual writing, AI outline, AI draft) experiment (N = 388), participants assigned to present extraversion rated themselves as more extraverted than those assigned to present introversion (d = 0.32), and the size of this identity shift did not differ across authorship conditions. AI involvement changed the writing process. Participants in both AI conditions searched their memories more deliberately for fitting examples, and participants who edited an AI draft felt less ownership of their text than those who wrote from an AI outline. Neither process accounted for the shift. The presenter need not be the sole author of a self-presentation for it to shape self-perception.

articles.title: The FlexER-Scale: A new Self-report Measure of Individual Differences in Emotion Regulation Flexibility
articles.authors: Anne Gärtner; Christoph Scheffel; Timo Schweikert; Denise Dörfel
articles.abstract: Previous research on emotion regulation (ER) has primarily focused on individual strategies and their association with well-being and psychopathology. Recent frameworks emphasize a context-sensitive, goal-dependent approach, defining ER flexibility as the ability to adaptively adjust ER strategies based on contextual demands and personal goals. Despite growing evidence for its relevance, a concise self-report measure designed to capture trait-level, strategy-independent ER flexibility has been lacking. To address this gap, we developed the Flexible Emotion Regulation Scale (FlexER-Scale) and validated it using data from four independent samples (N = 1,019). Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) in an independent sample examined the scale’s structure; criterion validity was assessed via correlations with the WHO-5 Well-Being Index and the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ). The final 10-item FlexER-Scale demonstrated good psychometric properties, including satisfactory item discrimination and high internal consistency (α = .85). EFA suggested a two-factor structure differentiating hedonic and contra-hedonic ER flexibility, which was supported by CFA. The FlexER-Scale showed a significant positive correlation with psychological well-being, driven by the hedonic factor. Small but significant correlations with habitual reappraisal and suppression use provided initial evidence for discriminant validity. The FlexER-Scale is a promising tool for assessing ER flexibility, offering a concise alternative to existing measures by capturing adaptive regulatory variability without relying on predefined strategies. Future research should examine its construct validity, longitudinal stability, and predictive validity. Given that the validation was based on predominantly student samples from a German-speaking context, broader generalizability remains to be established.

articles.title: Challenges and opportunities in emotion dynamics research:  an interdisciplinary perspective
articles.authors: N. Vasileiadis; Daouia Larabi; Peter de Jonge; Klaas J Wardenaar
articles.abstract: Recent advances in the acquisition of intensive longitudinal data (ILD) have enabled affective science to investigate emotional experience in increasingly ecologically valid contexts. These developments highlight the complexity of psychological systems and the challenges involved in understanding emotions. In this perspective paper, we argue for a conceptual adjustment in how measurement is practiced in emotion-dynamics research. Drawing on affective science, computational modeling, and the philosophy of science, we propose that measurement should be treated as an interaction that may partially structure and modify the phenomenon being measured. This perspective has implications for the design, acquisition, and analysis of ILD. We identify three complementary directions for future research. First, measurement frameworks should be theory-informed and transparent, with methodological choices and relevant hyperparameters explicitly documented to support cumulative science. Second, subjective self-report should be complemented, where appropriate, by behavioral, physiological, and environmental measures to provide partially independent perspectives on complex psychological processes. Third, greater attention should be given to temporal scale in ILD measurement and analysis, including multiscale dynamical network approaches that connect proximal, observable, and potentially perturbable processes with higher-level psychological phenomena. Together, these directions support a shift from describing statistical associations toward a more process-oriented understanding of psychological phenomena.

articles.title: Testing different metrics for syntactic and morphological complexity in aphasic discourse: A cross-genre comparison in Spanish
articles.authors: Jorge Ricardo Hidalgo Chagoya; Xabi Ansorena; Roel Jonkers; Maddi Carrera; Ignacio Quemada Ubis; Simona Mancini
articles.abstract:
Purpose: The aim of this study is to determine which of four tasks testing different discourse genres (descriptive, procedural, conversational, and narrative) is the most sensitive in detecting syntactic and morphological complexity deficits in Spanish aphasia. Additionally, we compare two approaches for measuring syntax in discourse to identify the most accurate set of metrics for discriminating group membership.

Method: In this comparative cross-sectional study, we analyzed the discourse of an aphasia group (N = 20) and a non-brain-damaged group (N = 14). Data was preprocessed using manual and automated procedures. We measured syntactic complexity through proxies (mean length of utterance, noun-verb ratio, and verbs per utterance), in addition to a competing ‘syntactic structures’ metric. The latter includes variables of subordination, left branching, relative clauses, and word integration, while morphological complexity was measured through an inflectional index.

Results: The descriptive and narrative tasks highlighted the most significant differences across syntactic complexity metrics between the groups. Additionally, nested binomial logistic regression models showed that the ‘syntactic structures’ metric predicted groups better than the proxies alone.

Conclusions: A comprehensive assessment of syntactic complexity can be obtained through the administration of both descriptive and narrative tasks. The measurement of ‘syntactic structures’ in discourse proved a fitter and more fine-grained approach for group discrimination than the incorporation of syntactic proxies alone. These findings provide guidance for a precise discourse assessment in Spanish aphasia.

articles.title: Affect and Self–Other Risk Judgments: Evidence for Target-Invariant Influence
articles.authors: Erik Hallberg; Pär Bjälkebring; Magnus Bergquist
articles.abstract: Affective evaluations play a central role in risk perception, yet it remains unclear whether affect shapes judgments differently when risks are evaluated for oneself versus others. Across two studies, we tested whether hazard-directed affect exerts a differential influence on self-focused and other-focused risk judgments. Study 1 (N = 77) featured a repeated-measures design in which participants rated affect, perceived risk, and perceived benefit for 13 technologies for themselves and for a random other, allowing within-person comparisons of self- and other-focused judgments. A linear mixed-effects model indicated that although negative affect predicted higher perceived risk and positive affect predicted lower perceived risk, the influence of affect did not differ across judgment targets. With the same design, Study 2 (N = 150) experimentally manipulated hazard-directed affect using negatively versus positively valenced images across five technologies. The positive affect manipulation lowered perceived risk while negative affect increased perceived risk. The influence of the manipulation did not differ across judgment targets. Additionally, we examined whether the inverse association between perceived risk and perceived benefit, an indicator of the affect heuristic, varied by target: evidence for a stronger inverse association for other-focused judgments emerged in Study 1, suggesting affective cues may be relied upon more readily when making judgements for others. This finding did not replicate in Study 2. Together, our findings refine affect-based accounts of risk perception by suggesting affective evaluations of hazards are applied similarly across judgment targets, even when self–other differences in risk level are present.

articles.title: A Relevance Rate Model of the affective mechanisms linking social media use to later attentional disruption
articles.authors: Hippolyte Fournier; eva pool; David Sander; Elise Dan-Glauser
articles.abstract: Social media use is increasingly suspected of harming attention, but the evidence remains too limited to draw any firm conclusions. One obstacle is the lack of a framework specifying how such use might affect attention afterwards, without any device. To address this gap, we draw on emotional attention, the affective mechanism that prioritises what matters to individuals. The Relevance Rate Model rests on the relevance rate, the frequency with which an environment delivers concern-relevant stimuli. Drawing on predictive coding, we suggest that social media raises the rate that users expect, and that this expectation may persist after each session and, with repeated use, across daily life. When an activity delivers less concern-relevant information than expected, sustained attention to the ongoing task may be disrupted as emotional attention is recruited to address the shortfall. The model specifies four measurable parameters of use, from which we derive a research agenda.

articles.title: The Benefits of and Motivations Behind Large-Team Coordination in Psychology
articles.authors: Sajedeh Rasti; Krist Vaesen; Daniel Lakens
articles.abstract: To increase coordination in science in areas where this would be beneficial for knowledge generation, collaborative work needs to offer clear benefits to individual researchers. This study investigates the motivations for initiating large-team papers and the potential benefits of these projects in psychology. By qualitatively analyzing 500 papers, we find that large-team collaborations are most often instigated to deal with the practical challenges  inherent to complex research questions, but can also be motivated by broader social and or strategic factors. The results from quantitatively analyzing 1,699,513 papers published between 1975 and 2024 indicate that large-team collaborations are more likely to be cited and to appear in higher-ranked journals. Furthermore, their immediate impact on the field, as measured by citation counts within the first 2 years after publication, is on average higher than individually-authored papers. This suggests that contributing to collaborative projects in psychology will likely increase the number of high-rank journal publications to the resume of researchers. Overall, our findings indicate that large-team collaborations can be rewarding for individual researchers both by enabling early scientific impact and by contributing to stronger publication records.

articles.title: Can AI Scale Human Fact-Checking? Evidence from Community Notes
articles.authors: Thomas Renault; Mohsen Mosleh; David Gertler Rand
articles.abstract: Community Notes---a crowd-based fact-checking program through which social media users can flag a post with a note explaining why the post is misleading, and the note is displayed if a diverse set of users rate the note as helpful---has become central to online content moderation. The program, however, faces substantial scalability constraints, as the generation of notes takes considerable time and effort, and the number of user participants is limited. Here, we investigate whether allowing AI models to write Community Notes helps to alleviate these constraints by analyzing the full corpus of AI-generated Community Notes on X through May 2026. Encouragingly, AI-generated notes are submitted more quickly, are longer, and cite more and higher-quality sources than human-written notes, while being rated helpful at a similar rate and being associated with similar decreases in reposts following the publication of a rated-helpful note. Furthermore, a pre-registered survey experiment finds no statistically detectable difference between AI- and human-generated fact-checks in their effect on belief updating, regardless of whether the author was revealed to participants. On the other hand, AI-generated note writing is highly concentrated, as a handful of accounts produce the large majority of notes, and are significantly less likely to engage with posts involving controversial and polarized topics such as politics and elections. While those findings suggest that AI may be a powerful tool for scaling crowd-based fact-checking systems such as Community Notes, this evolution also entails important risks: shifting the primary bottleneck from note production to note evaluation, moving the system from a decentralized toward a more centralized model, and creating incentives to prioritize claims that are more likely to achieve consensus over those of greater societal importance.

articles.title: Predicting Personality Traits from Short Unstructured Conversations with AI
articles.authors: Daniel Robert Lametti; Ileana Wheeler; Jonah Appleton; Robin Murphy; Santiago Castiello
articles.abstract: Given the complexity of personality, we might assume that significant behaviour is required to express our traits. Here we use large language models (LLMs) to test the extent to which personality is visible in short conversations with artificial intelligence (AI). In a preregistered experiment, 100 participants completed the Big Five Inventory (BFI) before having unstructured conversations with GPT-4.1, writing a median of 430 words. We then instructed a second LLM rater (Claude Sonnet 4.6) to complete the BFI as if it were each participant, predicting their responses based solely on an analysis of the participant-GPT chats. Correlations between LLM-predicted and self-reported BFI traits were significant (range r = .25 to .47), in some cases matching previously documented self-other predictions from family members. A linguistic analysis revealed that the LLM rater’s predictions relied largely on lexical content as opposed to syntax. Using preexisting data, we tested if the AI’s persona influenced how much participants revealed about themselves in conversation. A hundred participants chatted with two versions of GPT-4.1—one that mirrored their personality (mirror AI) and one that opposed it (inverse AI). The LLM rater predicted BFI traits based on the interactions and we correlated this prediction with self-report. Mirror chats generated significant correlations, averaging r = .41; for inverse chats the average fell to r = .30, and dropped to zero when the prediction relied on lexical content alone. People readily convey their personality profile in short conversations with AI, and this is enhanced when the AI’s persona mirrors the users.

articles.title: Cognitive Model Organism: The Unboxing of Thinking Process
articles.authors: Yuncheng Jia; Bo Qin; Anuchit Phanumartwiwath
articles.abstract: We establish the Hortus Regis Alti (HRA) Experimental and Observational Protocol for studying a frozen language model as a cognitive model organism. The preparation combines controlled input perturbations, complete native-token preservation, deterministic symbolic probes, contextual process coding, and explicit failure screening. One DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B implementation with INT8 linear layers and BF16 elsewhere produced 176 archived trajectories across four observation configurations of one Bayesian decision problem, containing 2,205,963 generated tokens. Eight baseline pairs regenerated identical overlapping prefixes across 93,016 token positions. Three empirical demonstrations organize the study. Symbolic closure separated from execution termination, including renewed processing after a closure marker. Aggregate consumption separated from item-specific response paths: 36 of 40 four-level item series changed direction. Correct local computation separated from maintenance of task representation: an auxiliary result could be calculated correctly and subsequently rebound as an operand. Complete contextual reading localized 1,926 evidence anchors, including successful repairs and recurrent failures. Measurement checks further showed that a short window could classify a long exact cycle as highly diverse. These findings motivate testable hypotheses of representational control competition, training-register capture, and content-specific effects of symbolic continuation. The contribution is a process-oriented experimental preparation, a reproducible trajectory collection, and a quality-control procedure that connects observable symbolic events to discriminating intervention sites. Precision specifications identify the model strain, execution conditions, measurement units, semantic coding decisions, and regeneration range supporting these claims.

articles.title: Two Decades of Reading Performance at the Alouette Test: Descriptive Data and Dyslexia  Screening Properties in French Primary School Children
articles.authors: DUCROT; Brice Brossette; Tom Chetrit; Bernard Lété
articles.abstract:
Background: The Alouette test is widely used in France to assess reading performance and screen for dyslexia. Its low semantic predictability text limits contextual compensation and emphasizes word identification. However, its 2005 standardization relied on small grade-level samples, evidence on its screening properties in school-age children remains limited, and temporal changes in performance are poorly documented. 
Methods: We pooled 5,118 Alouette assessment records from typically developing French-speaking children in Grades 1–5, collected across research projects between 2004 and 2025. We examined grade and sex differences and associations with school socioeconomic status. Screening properties were evaluated in 744 children with a prior diagnosis of developmental dyslexia and 744 matched controls. Temporal associations were examined using regression models accounting for grade, sex, and school socioeconomic status, with school-level clustering addressed where appropriate. Sensitivity analyses examined age and school composition, and exploratory models compared gradual trends with change around 2018, when French educational reforms placed renewed emphasis on foundational reading skills and structured phonics. 
Results: Performance improved across grades on all indices except errors, with no substantial sex differences. Associations with school socioeconomic status were stronger in the upper grades. Children with dyslexia performed more poorly on all indices. The areas under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves were .861 for reading accuracy and .902 for reading efficiency. At grade-specific 10th-percentile thresholds, reading efficiency yielded 76.3% sensitivity and 88.6% specificity. Across assessment years, reading efficiency increased by about 0.6% per year on average, whereas accuracy declined slightly, mainly in Grades 1 and 2. Exploratory models favored a difference of approximately 9% in reading efficiency between observations collected before and after 2018 over a single linear trend, although patterns varied across indices.
Conclusions: This study provides extensive descriptive data on Alouette performance and evidence of its potential for dyslexia screening. The proposed thresholds require independent validation before routine clinical use. Retrospective sampling and discontinuous temporal coverage limit generalizability, and the observed post-2018 difference cannot be attributed with certainty to education reforms.

articles_hidden.title: Project EMPOWER-ED: A Pilot Study of an Online Single-Session Intervention for Caregivers of Youth Hospitalized with Anorexia Nervosa
articles_hidden.authors: Ariela Kaiser; Arielle C. Smith; Lauren Swift; Jenna Yejin Sung; Jocelyn Lebow; Jessica L. Schleider
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: Caregivers play a crucial role in the treatment of children and adolescents with anorexia nervosa (AN), but often report uncertainty about how to respond effectively to the illness, particularly during transitions from higher to lower levels of care.  Single-session interventions (SSIs) offer a promising approach to addressing this gap while minimizing burden on caregivers during this particularly stressful period of time. This study describes the feasibility and acceptability of a brief web-based caregiver SSI targeting accommodation of eating disorder behaviors. Method: Participants included caregivers of patients admitted for inpatient medical stabilization treatment of AN. Prior to their child’s discharge, caregivers completed surveys and the Project EMPOWER-ED SSI. Result: Feasibility of Project EMPOWER-ED was high, with 89% of possible participants enrolling and completing the intervention along with pre-to-post questionnaires, and of those, 72% providing optional qualitative feedback. On a 5-point scale, caregivers reported a 0.48-point (SD=1.01) increase in their preparedness to help their child manage eating disorder-related distress and a 0.56-point (SD=0.87) increase in their ability to manage their child’s eating disorder-related distress, from pre- to post-intervention. Overall, caregivers found the intervention to be highly acceptable, with qualitative feedback highlighting a number of likely contributors, including practical content, feeling validated, and the digital, self-guided format. Discussion: Overall, results suggested that Project EMPOWER-ED had high uptake and completion rates, high overall ratings of acceptability, and promising preliminary changes on measures of caregivers’ perceived preparedness to tolerate their child’s distress.

articles_hidden.title: mirtverse: Accessible, AI-ready Item Response Theory in R with mirt
articles_hidden.authors: Okan Bulut
articles_hidden.abstract: Item response theory (IRT) is the statistical foundation of most modern tests: It links the responses people give to  test items with the latent trait the test is meant to measure, and it underpins item banking, test assembly, computerized adaptive testing, score linking and fairness analyses (de Ayala, 2022; Embretson & Reise, 2000; Lord, 1980). The R environment (R Core Team, 2026) offers many IRT packages, and among them mirt (Chalmers, 2012) stands out for the breadth of models and estimation methods it supports. Its power comes with a cost, however: Choosing, checking, interpreting and reporting a model in mirt requires fluency in both R and psychometrics. mirtverse (Bulut, 2026b) is an R package that sits on top of mirt and makes it usable by a wider audience. It turns fitted mirt models into tidy tables, publication-ready ggplot2 graphics (Wickham, 2016), plain-language interpretations, item health cards, one-file HTML reports, and shareable dashboards. A point-and-click Shiny workbench runs the same functions and writes the R code for every step. Beyond the usual IRT toolkit, mirtverse adds a generative AI layer that writes analysis scripts from a plain-language request, drafts and verifies test items, trains and audits automated scorers for open-ended responses, and predicts item difficulty from item text. Every AI feature sits behind a psychometric check, so a language model can speed up the work but cannot quietly lower its standards. The package is accompanied by an open textbook (Bulut, 2026a), ten interactive teaching labs, and an instructor toolkit. This paper reviews the theory that mirtverse builds on, the current landscape of IRT software in R, the reasons for building on mirt, and the design of mirtverse, including its AI capabilities.

articles_hidden.title: Examining Factors that Influence Acceptability of Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy: Experimental and Correlational Approaches
articles_hidden.authors: Claire Whiting; Jesus A. Arroyo; Erik C Nook
articles_hidden.abstract: Objectives. Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) are widely used treatments that aim to increase clients' awareness and acceptance of their present-moment experiences. Although delivered as secular treatments, their practices have roots in East and South Asian religious traditions, raising concerns about acceptance among diverse religious or atheistic clients. Other MBI features, such as meditation and group-based formats, may also pose barriers to participation. We report two pre-registered experiments examining factors influencing acceptability of Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT). Methods. Study 1 (N = 305) tested whether scientific versus religious framings of MBCT influenced treatment acceptability, and whether effects were moderated by religiosity, existential quest (tendency toward exploratory engagement with existential questions), and scriptural literalism. Study 2 (N = 705) examined whether addressing participants' concerns about MBCT increased acceptability. Results. Contrary to hypotheses, Study 1 found no effects of scientific or religious framing on acceptability. However, regardless of framing, MBCT acceptability was higher among participants with greater existential quest (significantly) and greater religiosity (marginally). In Study 2, addressing participants' concerns (whether tailored to their specific concerns or covering all possible concerns) reduced concerns about MBCT and increased acceptability relative to no intervention. Similar to Study 1, religiosity was positively associated with acceptability regardless of condition. Conclusions. Together, these findings suggest that religiosity and existential quest may shape receptivity to MBCT, and that addressing client concerns, rather than adjusting how treatment is framed, may offer a promising route to increasing acceptability. Understanding these individual differences can inform strategies for engaging diverse populations in MBIs.

articles_hidden.title: Is it time for teacher education to include a nature-based commitment?
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah MacQuarrie; Clare Nugent; Rebecca Phillips; Elizabeth Birchinall; Alexandra Hennessey
articles_hidden.abstract: Teacher education increasingly recognises that meaningful outdoor learning depends on teachers’ own relationships with nature, yet many enter the profession with limited confidence or formative outdoor experience. Research shows that children’s nature engagement and conservation sensibilities are shaped by the dispositions of the adults who teach them, signalling the need for programmes that nurture teachers’ ecological familiarity, interpretive skill and place-based confidence. However, structural barriers inhibit sustained practice, producing inequitable provision across schools. Teachers experience tensions between curriculum-driven expectations and the slower, contemplative qualities of outdoor learning, such as dwell time, sensory exploration and unstructured observation. Inclusive outdoor practice further relies on knowledgeable staff capable of supporting diverse learners. The role of place, context and culturally shaped nature orientations remains fundamental and requires scrutiny for outdoor learning to move into sustained practice. Collectively, these insights highlight the need for a systemic, nature-based commitment within teacher education that develops teacher confidence, addresses contextual constraints and expands pedagogical possibilities outdoors.

articles_hidden.title: Testing the solitary drinking component of the social-contextual framework for AUD risk among young adults using Directed Acyclic Graphs
articles_hidden.authors: Connor James Smith; Jonas Dora; Mikela Ritter; Kasey Creswell; Kevin Michael King
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: Solitary drinking is a low base rate behavior present in some young adults that could be an indicator for the development of later alcohol use problems. The present work will use a combination of observational data, Directed Acyclic Graphs, and latent variable models to test a between-person causal model of the role of solitary drinking in the etiology of alcohol use disorder risk in young adults. Method: Participants were young adults at baseline (n = 496, aged 18–22, Mage = 20.3, SD = 1.3) recruited from the Pacific Northwest who reported drinking or using cannabis “about once per week” or more over the past three months. Participants completed a baseline assessment and about 32 days of ecological momentary assessments, answering questions about negative emotionality, social withdrawal, urgency, and their alcohol use.  Results: will be added at Stage 2. Conclusions: will be added at Stage 2.

articles_hidden.title: Maladaptive Precision: A Channel-Specific Predictive-Processing Framework for the Neurodevelopmental Consequences of Early Life Adversity
articles_hidden.authors: Martin Gerbert Frasch; Bea Van den Bergh
articles_hidden.abstract: Early life adversity (ELA) is proposed here to bias precision weighting in specific information channels, up-weighting potential threat and predictable input while down-weighting evidence that disconfirms expectations of danger, rather than altering a single global gain. We ground this predictive-processing (PP) claim in developmental neuroscience: calibration occurs within critical and sensitive periods whose molecular brakes, together with self-confirming patterns of evidence sampling, can stabilize precision settings beyond the conditions that produced them, and susceptibility to calibration varies between individuals. We distinguish the parsimonious core claim (altered precision) from a stronger, optional claim (entrenched maladaptive priors) and specify behavioral, computational, and neural signatures that dissociate them. A mapping table links dimensions of early experience (threat, deprivation, unpredictability, rigid invariance, prenatal maternal distress, and supportive caregiving) to predicted precision channels, developmental windows, measurable indices, and disconfirming observations. Mechanistically, we propose the anterior cingulate cortex as a hub for allocating gain across channels within a distributed circuit that includes the amygdala, insula, orbitofrontal and ventromedial prefrontal cortex, striatum, thalamus, and the noradrenergic, cholinergic, and dopaminergic systems, and we state what each node contributes. Apparently contradictory findings, threat-related hyper-reactivity alongside reduced reward-prediction-error encoding, are read as one biased allocation of gain. The framework is held to a symmetry constraint (supportive input should confer faster precision re-tuning), states its boundary conditions, and yields falsifiable predictions and testable implications for exposure-based, pharmacological, and caregiving interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Do Incarceration and Release Change How People Treat Those With a Criminal History? Longitudinal Behavioural and Neural Evidence.
articles_hidden.authors: Victoria RAMBAUD; Ilke Veeckman; Louis Favril; Tom Vander Beken; Emilie A. Caspar
articles_hidden.abstract: Social decision-making is central to successful reintegration following incarceration, yet whether imprisonment changes how people treat individuals with versus without a criminal history remains unclear. In this preregistered longitudinal study, newly detained (incoming, n = 34) and newly released (outgoing, n = 13) individuals completed a social decision task with EEG at three sessions over eight months, choosing whether to direct prosocial or antisocial actions toward characters described as having an incarceration history (here termed incarceration-history targets) or not (community targets). Frontal midline theta (FMθ) was recorded as an index of choice-related conflict. Prison-climate and quality-of-life measures were also collected. Across groups, participants identified more strongly with (formerly) incarcerated individuals, yet directed more antisocial intentions toward incarceration-history targets and more prosocial intentions toward community targets. Incoming participants showed a reduction in prosocial community intentions after four months that rebounded by eight months. Incoming participants showed higher FMθ than outgoing participants early in incarceration, with a progressive reduction over time in all groups, consistent with reduced decision conflict. Exploratory analyses linked social intentions to prison-environment and well-being factors. Because the target types differed in criminal history and, inevitably, in how positively they were described, these effects are best understood as responses to stigma linked with incarceration-history rather than to group membership. These findings suggest that incarceration and release involve distinct adaptations in social decision-making toward (ex-)prisoners, with dissociable behavioural and neural markers.

articles_hidden.title: How many sounds is a picture worth? A dual process perspective on the differences between memory for environmental sounds and pictures
articles_hidden.authors: Colleen M Parks; Laura Lucille Sarah Werner; Margaret Ann McMullin; Joel S. Snyder
articles_hidden.abstract: Recognition memory on standard old/new tests is typically better for pictures than for sounds. To investigate this modality effect, we examined the contributions of recollection and familiarity processes to recognition memory of auditory and visual objects (environmental sounds and colored line drawings, respectively). To gain some insight into the source of the modality difference, we investigated whether the modality effect was larger for one process than the other. Indeed, in Experiment 1, recollection was greater for visual than auditory objects, but the modality effect on familiarity was much smaller. We replicated this pattern in all subsequent experiments. Focusing on recollection, we examined the consequences of hindering encoding during study with a divided attention task. Surprisingly, Experiments 2 - 4 showed that divided attention at study substantially reduced visual recollection but had little effect on auditory recollection, to the point that visual recollection in the divided attention condition was similar to auditory recollection in the full attention condition. This unusually small effect of divided attention on auditory recollection aligns with prior research showing fundamental differences in recognition of sounds and pictures.  Further, it suggests that effects we have taken as regularities in recognition (such as divided attention) may not apply to all modalities.

articles_hidden.title: Short-Term Effects on Parenting and Adolescent Well-Being of a Personalized Digital Parenting Intervention. A Randomized Controlled Trial
articles_hidden.authors: Rick van Logchem; Crystal R. Smit; Anne Bülow; Savannah Boele; Bart Soenens; Loes Keijsers
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: To counter increasing youth mental health problems, it has been suggested to invest in broadly accessible parenting programs. To date, few online parenting programs exist and the majority provide universal rather than personalized advice. This preregistered randomized controlled trial tested a novel digital parenting intervention, composed of self-monitoring of parenting, a data-driven parenting report, and 6 weeks of online parenting tips to stimulate need-supportive parenting.
Methods: This preregistered study compared post-intervention parenting (proximal outcome) and adolescent affective well-being (distal outcome) of 321 families in a control condition (100 daily diaries), with 225 families in an intervention group who additionally received a feedback report and add-on parenting tips from day 50 onwards. The report and tips were either universal (n = 107) or personalized (n = 110). This trial was registered at the CCMO: NL-009451 on 19-02-2025 [https://www.onderzoekmetmensen.nl/en/trial/57487]
Results: Throughout the study, parents became less need-supportive, but adolescents experienced their parents as more need-supportive. Both parents and adolescents observed decreased overparenting over time. Parents in the control group reported becoming less autonomy supportive and warm (pre-post intervention) which was not found in the intervention groups. Adolescents in the universal intervention group perceived an increase in structure over time and an increase in negative affect (mainly irritability). No significant group differences were detected however (p’s > .06). Hence, an additional 6 weeks of parenting tips and a feedback report (our intervention) did not outperform the impact of 100 days of self-monitoring.
Conclusions: Digital self-monitoring of parenting, combined with data-driven feedback and online parenting tips, seems to make parents more critical of their own parenting, but leaves adolescents more satisfied with the need-supportiveness of their parents. Moreover, this online parenting intervention, designed to target need-supportiveness, might counter harmful overparenting practices.

articles_hidden.title: The answer is yes. But what was the question? Towards more useful theories in sport and exercise psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Maik Bieleke; Lorenz Assländer; Wanja Wolff
articles_hidden.abstract: Debates about reform in sport and exercise psychology research largely center on the shortcomings of null hypothesis significance testing (NHST) and the binary conclusions it produces. We argue that significance testing is not the main culprit. NHST matches our theories, which typically use boxes and arrows to state that an effect exists and in which direction. So changing the statistical tool we use does not change much of what we learn, because it does not alter the questions we pursue or the specificity of the predictions we make: the answers we seek and settle for remain yes or no. The good news is that sport and exercise psychology is in a strong position to tackle more informative questions: We have established that many effects exist, collected a wealth of quantitatively rich data, and have sophisticated methods at hand. What is missing is a place in our theories to put these numbers. We outline three increasingly ambitious levers to transform this foundation into a more quantitative body of knowledge: (1) treating effect sizes and their precision as primary targets of study planning and inference, rather than as decorative statistics reported alongside the p-value; (2) synthesizing evidence cumulatively, so that established findings such as expected effect sizes constrain the next study; and (3) formulating theories themselves more quantitatively, for instance regarding the shape of a relationship or how quickly an effect unfolds, so that they make more precise predictions. Doing so benefits scientists and practitioners alike. Theories that make precise predictions can actually be wrong, which is what makes confirmations meaningful. A focus on cumulative effect size estimation also means that every well-conducted study teaches us something irrespective of its p-value, including the questions practitioners care about most: how much an intervention is likely to help, for whom, and when.

articles_hidden.title: Motivational Incongruence Predicts Subsequent Psychological Distress in Psychotherapy: Within-Person Evidence From Three Samples
articles_hidden.authors: Leo Bornhauser; Max Lustenberger; Juan Martín Gómez Penedo; Wolfgang Lutz; Antonia Lanning; Thomas Berger; Franz Caspar; Martin grosse Holtforth
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: Motivational incongruence refers to insufficient satisfaction of individual motives in interaction with the environment and is assumed to contribute to psychological distress and psychopathology when prolonged. This study examined reduced motivational incongruence as a potential change mechanism in psychotherapy by testing whether within-person decreases in motivational incongruence predict subsequent decreases in general psychological distress. Method: Analyses were based on three psychotherapy samples from two randomized controlled trials and one observational dataset collected in routine care, comprising 1,656 patients in total. In each sample, motivational incongruence and distress were assessed at four to six occasions during treatment using short forms of the Incongruence Questionnaire and the Symptom Checklist-90-R, respectively. Random-intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPMs) tested prospective within-person effects between motivational incongruence and distress. Latent curve models with structured residuals (LCM-SRs) served as exploratory robustness analyses. Results: Across three samples, the RI-CLPMs yielded significant and large prospective effects of motivational incongruence on subsequent distress. Reverse cross-lagged effects, from distress to subsequent motivational incongruence, were significant in two of the three samples. The exploratory LCM-SR supported the primary motivational incongruence-to-distress effect in one sample but yielded no admissible solutions in the other two. Conclusions: Across three independent psychotherapy samples, within-person reductions in motivational incongruence preceded reductions in distress, consistent with motivational incongruence as a potential transtheoretical change mechanism in psychotherapy. Motivational incongruence may therefore represent a candidate treatment target. Future research should test the proposed causal relationship experimentally and examine which dimensions of motivational incongruence are most relevant for individual patients.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive Control as Precision Regulation: From Predictive Coding to Adaptive Behaviou
articles_hidden.authors: Enrico Giraldi; Riccardo Proietti; Giovanni Pezzulo
articles_hidden.abstract:
Cognitive control is traditionally conceptualized as a set of top-down mechanisms that select
and regulate stimulus–response mappings to support goal-directed and flexible behaviour.
Traditional accounts have provided fundamental insights into the neural architecture of
cognitive control and identified a set of core control processes, including goal maintenance, task
switching, control allocation, conflict monitoring, and cognitive effort. However, they rarely
address how these functions can be integrated within a common computational architecture.
Furthermore, most theories tend to assume that the core control functions use specialized
mechanisms that are fundamentally distinct from those supporting action–perception loops.
Here, we review an alternative perspective grounded in predictive coding and active inference,
according to which cognitive control emerges from hierarchical elaborations of the same
generative inference supporting perception and action. Within predictive coding and active
inference, the brain continuously generates predictions about sensory inputs, actions, and
their expected consequences, and updates these predictions on the basis of precision-weighted
prediction errors. We argue that the same precision-weighting mechanism, when operating
beyond sensory processing—to optimize the precision of higher-level beliefs and of courses of
action (policies)—provides the foundations of cognitive control, allowing a cognitive system to
balance the stability of current goals and task representations against the flexibility required
to respond to unexpected information and environmental changes. From this perspective, the
core control processes emerge as different facets of precision regulation within a hierarchical
generative model: the precision of higher-level beliefs supports goal maintenance and task
switching; policy precision supports control allocation, setting the balance between habitual
and goal-directed control and prioritizing the latter when required by task demands; conflict
monitoring provides information about whether the selected policy continues to produce
expected and preferred outcomes; and cognitive effort reflects the cost of increasing precision to
change the resulting control configuration. Finally, we link the precision-based computations to
putative neural processes in frontoparietal networks and neuromodulatory processes spanning
dopaminergic, noradrenergic, and cholinergic systems, and derive empirical predictions that
can test the proposed framework.

articles_hidden.title: Malevolent Creativity and the Dark Tetrad – (Plenty of) Null Findings for Idea Generation Tasks
articles_hidden.authors: Corinna Perchtold-Stefan; Christian Rominger; Andreas Fink; David H Cropley
articles_hidden.abstract: Past research has strongly emphasized the role of dark personality, particularly, the dark triad/tetrad in malevolent creativity. However, reported associations largely stem from self-report measures (e.g., the Malevolent Creativity Behavior Scale: MCBS), which has received criticism. For this reason, in two-independent studies, this paper scrutinizes the relevance of the dark triad/tetrad for performance in a malevolent creativity test (MCT). Associations were tested for total malevolent creativity, and followed up for originality, malevolence, and fluency of ideas. In study 1 (n = 307), neither correlations nor multiple regression models revealed any significant association of narcissism, Machiavellianism, or psychopathy with malevolent creativity performance metrics. In study 2 (n = 287), correlations between the dark tetrad and MCT creativity metrics were equally non-significant. Only in multiple regression models, a combination of high Machiavellianism, high psychopathy, and high sadism (three-way interaction) predicted higher total malevolent creativity.
