Overall, associations with MCT creativity metrics did not surpass small effects of f² = 0.02, showing that the apparently robust findings from malevolent creativity self-report do not replicate in malevolent creativity performance tests. It is thus possible that the dark triad/tetrad may be less relevant for malevolent idea generation that previously assumed.

articles_hidden.title: Identifying Causal Effects in Experiments with Latent Treatments: An Instrumental Variable Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Lukas Junker; Florian Pargent
articles_hidden.abstract:
Psychological experiments target the causal effects of latent variables, which they cannot manipulate directly. Researchers use manipulation checks to confirm that the latent variable changed, but then estimate the causal effect of the manipulation itself, not that of changes in the target latent variable. We treat the manipulation as an instrumental variable (IV) for the latent treatment, measured by several items, and derive conditions under which the treatment's average causal effect is identified. The resulting assumptions allow for some treatment-effect and loading heterogeneity, and are weaker than those most psychometric applications already make.

Because a latent treatment has no unit, the estimand is defined only once a scale is fixed. We define two and work out their identification: an anchored estimand, per unit of one item, and a standardized estimand, per standard deviation of the latent treatment. The latter is more familiar but requires more assumptions and, notably, does not transfer between experiments. We show how to estimate both estimands with off-the-shelf SEM and IV software, and a simulation shows how the estimators behave in realistic samples when individual assumptions fail. Because researchers design the manipulation and choose the items, we close with practical implications.

articles_hidden.title: Gendergerecht oder Gendergaga? Eine Metaanalyse über den Einfluss von geschlechtergerechten Formulierungen auf das Lesen
articles_hidden.authors: Katharina Marie Bach; Amadeus J. Pickal; Veronika Wachholz; Constanze Richters; Julia Murböck; Laura Brandl; Matthias Stadler; Michael Sailer
articles_hidden.abstract:
Geschlechtergerechte Sprache wird medial, politisch und gesellschaftlich kontrovers diskutiert. Befürworterinnen und Befürworter möchten alle Geschlechter sprachlich repräsentieren und dem male bias durch das generische Maskulinum entgegenwirken. Im Gegensatz dazu befürchten Kritikerinnen und Kritiker negative Auswirkungen auf das Lesen. Bisher fehlen eindeutige Forschungsergebnisse zum Einfluss von geschlechtergerechter Sprache auf subjektive Textwahrnehmung und objektives Textverständnis. Daher aggregiert die vorliegende Metaanalyse Daten von 24 bisher unpublizierten Primärstudien mit insgesamt 922 Teilnehmerinnen und Teilnehmern, welche den Einfluss verschiedener geschlechtergerechter Formulierungen im Vergleich zum generischen Maskulinum auf die subjektive Textwahrnehmung (Güte der Formulierungen, Lesbarkeit, Verständlichkeit, kognitive Belastung) sowie das objektive Textverständnis (Erinnerungsleistung und Lesedauer) untersuchten. Zusätzlich untersuchte die Metaanalyse, ob die Art der geschlechtergerechten Formulierung (Gendersternchen, Binnen-I, Doppelpunkt, Beidnennung) die Effekte moderiert. Die Teilnehmerinnen und Teilnehmer der einzelnen Online-Studien wurden dafür randomisiert auf die verschiedenen Bedingungen aufgeteilt und mussten einen Text über die Schulschließungen während der Pandemie lesen und im Anschluss Fragebögen sowie einen auf den Text bezogenen Wissenstest ausfüllen. Diese schlechtere Bewertung der Verständlichkeit drückt möglicherweise die Skepsis gegenüber geschlechtergerechten Formulierungen aus. Menschen gewöhnen sich allerdings schnell an sprachliche Änderungen; eine regelmäßige Konfrontation kann im Sinne des Effekts der Darbietungshäufigkeit den Gewöhnungsprozess positiv beeinflussen.

articles_hidden.title: Adding 3D space to human navigation: Humans stop short of home after walking over a bridge
articles_hidden.authors: Charlotte Roy; Katharina Wünning; Timo Oess; Marc Ernst
articles_hidden.abstract: Human navigation has mostly been studied on flat ground, leaving open how elevation changes affect path integration. In two experiments, blindfolded participants reproduced the horizontal distance home after traversing flat paths, a bridge or stairs. Experiment 1 showed no detectable mean error after a straight flat path, but a substantial undershoot after the bridge. In Experiment 2, bridge and stair paths produced shorter returns relative to a straight-flat baseline than did a flat path matching the bridge’s profile; crawling over the bridge increased this undershoot. Participants overestimated bridge inclination and height. In Experiment 1, a horizontal projection based on perceived slopes descriptively covered approximately 74% of the group mean undershoot, without a detectable individual association. In Experiment 2, an exploratory perception–behaviour correlation did not survive correction for multiple comparisons, and homing errors showed no detectable inclination effect despite different perceptual predictions. Slope overestimation may therefore contribute to the undershoot, but its causal role remains unresolved. One interpretation is that humans integrate vertical movements metrically using biased inputs. The findings do not distinguish a 3D representation from projection onto a 2D representation.

articles_hidden.title: Testing working memory benefits long-term memory only when paired with re-exposure
articles_hidden.authors: Caro Hautekiet; T. LetkovÃ¡; Christian Nicolas Leon Olivers
articles_hidden.abstract: Testing long-term memory (LTM) is well known to enhance subsequent retention beyond mere re-exposure effects. Recent evidence suggests that testing during working memory (WM) also boosts LTM performance. However, it remains unclear whether these WM testing benefits are a consequence of retrieval or reflect increased familiarity due to re-exposure. In this preregistered study, we aimed to distinguish between these two. Participants memorized four images in their corresponding locations for a subsequent WM test. During this test, an image was presented in one of the memory locations, and participants had to determine whether it matched the memory (retrieval and re-exposure) or not (retrieval but no re-exposure). In an additional color-task condition, the image was presented in a red or green frame, but now participants simply determined the frame color (re-exposure only). Finally, in a no-test condition, no test was presented at all (neither retrieval nor re-exposure). Following an interruption, participants then completed a surprise LTM test involving a two-alternative forced-choice test between one old and one new image. LTM accuracy was higher for an item from the match condition than from the color-task condition, indicating a benefit of WM testing beyond re-exposure. Re-exposure alone also enhanced performance compared to no test. However, LTM performance in the non-matching test condition was no better than the no-test condition, suggesting that testing without re-exposure did not enhance LTM. Together, these findings suggest that while re-exposure benefits retention by itself, testing in WM boosts LTM only when paired with re-exposure to the target item.

articles_hidden.title: What Predicts Reading and Spelling in English as a Foreign Language? Cognitive and Linguistic Evidence from Young Learners in Germany
articles_hidden.authors: Heike Mlakar; Benjamin Goecke
articles_hidden.abstract: This longitudinal study examined which cognitive and linguistic skills predict English as a foreign language (EFL) reading and spelling skills among elementary school children in Germany. A total of 107 learners (Mage = 10.52, SD = 0.64) were assessed at the beginning of Grade 3 on nonverbal intelligence, phonological short-term memory, phonological awareness, working memory, and English grammar and vocabulary. Linear mixed-effects models, with age, gender, and language background as covariates and classes and schools as random effects, predicted six literacy outcomes at the end of Grade 4: reading comprehension, pseudoword reading, oral reading rate and accuracy, and real-word and pseudoword spelling. Nonverbal intelligence and phonological awareness predicted reading comprehension, and English vocabulary made a smaller contribution. Beyond comprehension, other outcomes showed different significant predictors: phonological short-term memory predicted pseudoword reading, L2 receptive grammar and vocabulary predicted real-word spelling, and nonverbal intelligence predicted pseudoword spelling. Phonological awareness, assessed in German, did not uniquely predict decoding or spelling, and no variable predicted oral reading rate or accuracy. The predictors differed across literacy outcomes, suggesting that early EFL reading and spelling components do not rest on a uniform set of skills.

articles_hidden.title: Sun safety at work: a needs assessment of occupational sun protection among outdoor workers in the Netherlands
articles_hidden.authors: Yara Y Sievers; Liesbeth van Osch; Rik Crutzen; Christel von Reeken; Nikee Driessens; Francine Schneider
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives: Outdoor workers face sustained exposure to ultraviolet radiation (UVR), increasing their skin cancer risk. This study reports a needs assessment concerning the health problem (sunburns and consequences), risk behaviours (inadequate sun protection), and underlying determinants among outdoor workers in the Netherlands.

Methods: Questionnaires (n=348) and semi-structured interviews (n=20) among outdoor workers in the Netherlands explored sunburn prevalence, occupational sun protection behaviours, and determinants.

Results: Outdoor workers reported high sunburn prevalences and insufficient occupational sun protection. Behavioural determinants included low perceived susceptibility and severity of sunburns and skin cancer, knowledge gaps, negative attitudes towards sun protection, perceived norms of individual autonomy, and the lack of supportive environments.

Conclusions: The results call for effective occupational sun protection strategies on the individual level and within workplace environments.

articles_hidden.title: Simulation-based cutoffs for conditional item fit in Rasch models: iterations, multiplicity correction, and decision stability
articles_hidden.authors: Magnus Johansson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Simulation-based cutoff values for conditional item fit can be estimated by parametric bootstrapping
and reported as an interval of a chosen width. Johansson (2025) recommended this
over rule-of-thumb critical values and gave iteration guidance based on detection rates and
conditioned on sample size, without an account of the error rate that the interval width controls.
This paper re-examines iterations and width against the familywise error rate (FWER),
and compares FWER and false discovery rate control. Seven simulation studies vary item count
and the targeting of misfitting items, with both dichotomous and polytomous conditions.

The interval width is shown to be the error rate parameter of the procedure, setting the
FWER jointly with the number of items. Bootstrap p-values with a Westfall-Young FWER
correction target that error rate directly, detect more misfit than a width-matched interval,
and are calibrated from 400 iterations, with fewer false positives than Benjamini-Hochberg.
Outfit was consistently less powerful than infit, confirming earlier dichotomous findings and
extending them to polytomous items.

Updated recommendations include flagging items on the Westfall-Young FWER corrected
p-value, using at least 400 iterations and 1000 to 2000 for a final analysis, and reporting the
interval as a descriptive band at width .95. The described methods are available in the R
package easyRasch2 and the jamovi module easyRasch2jmv.

articles_hidden.title: Towards a conceptual clarification and possible applications of Meehl’s crud factor: A preregistered systematic review
articles_hidden.authors: Robin Beckenbach; Ulrich S. Tran; Can Evenkamp; Susanne Kerschbaumer; Martin Voracek
articles_hidden.abstract: Paul E. Meehl’s crud factor posits that variables in the social and behavioural sciences are never entirely unrelated, encapsulated in the notion that “everything correlates with everything”. This preregistered systematic review examined how the crud factor and Lykken’s related concept of ambient noise have been defined, interpreted, and applied across research fields. We identified 424 works through database searches and citation tracking and analysed conceptual attributes and citation intentions. Among works allowing an inference about the relationship between the two concepts, the crud factor and ambient noise were almost uniformly treated as interchangeable, and both were most frequently invoked to argue that null-hypothesis significance testing against an exact-zero effect is unsuitable for corroborating theories. Reported numerical conventions for the crud factor varied widely, indicating no established empirical benchmark. Based on the synthesis, we propose an operational definition within the multitrait-multimethod validation framework: narrow-sense crud comprises heterotrait-heteromethod associations unexplained by substantive theory or theories of methodological artifacts, whereas broad-sense crud additionally encompasses heterotrait-monomethod associations and thus method-related covariance. This distinction provides a basis for empirically estimating the magnitude of the crud factor and evaluating its methodological implications.

articles_hidden.title: Transitions in Teachers’ Technology Utilization: Evidence from a Large-Scale, Longitudinal, and International Panel Study
articles_hidden.authors: Evi Konstantinidou; Ronny Scherer
articles_hidden.abstract: Teachers’ technology utilization varies substantially within and across educational systems, yet its longitudinal dynamics remain poorly understood. Using data from the International Computer and Information Literacy Study (ICILS) 2018-2020 Teacher Panel Study covering Denmark, Finland, and Uruguay, this study examined latent profiles of teachers’ ICT utilization, their stability and change over time, and associations with teacher characteristics. Profiles ranged from minimally engaged to comprehensive integrators, with intermediate profiles reflecting selective or functionally embedded ICT use. Two theoretically important profiles exhibited a paradoxical combination of positive ICT attitudes and low classroom practice, consistent with second-order barriers to technology integration. Profile stability varied cross-nationally, with Finland showing the greatest stability and Uruguay exhibiting a consolidation of profiles between occasions. ICT self-efficacy and collaborative ICT use were the most consistent predictors of lower-engagement profile membership. Our findings highlight cross-national heterogeneity in ICT utilization profiles and a persistent attitude-practice gap across educational systems. Effective professional development should target barriers preventing attitudinally committed teachers from enacting ICT in practice, with collaborative teaching cultures as a key enabling condition.

articles_hidden.title: Objective Neurocognitive Assessment of Stress and Recovery in Military Personnel: The NPRO-8 MIL Two-Tier Screening Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Jerome I. Rotgans
articles_hidden.abstract:
Prolonged military deployments expose personnel to sustained vigilance, disrupted sleep, uncertainty, repeated
high-consequence decisions, separation from social support, and restricted opportunities for recovery. Military
organizations routinely monitor physical fitness and medical readiness, but stress-related neurocognitive
functioning remains assessed primarily through self-report, observation, performance outcomes, and clinical
contact. These sources are indispensable, yet they may not reveal the physiological effort required to maintain
performance or the capacity to recover after cognitive demand. This paper introduces NPRO-8 MIL, a military
adaptation of the NPRO-8 Core mental-fitness screening framework. NPRO-8 MIL combines behavioral performance
with functional near-infrared spectroscopy during five structured cognitive task modules. Eight NeuroProbes inform
three higher-order pillars: Stress Load, Recovery Capacity, and Functional Impact. The underlying NPRO-8 Core has
completed internal validation through 178 deterministic tests, 32,000 Monte Carlo examinations, 50,850 repeated
robustness classifications, and parameter-sensitivity analyses. These findings establish computational coherence
and predictable behavior, while prospective military reliability, external-validity, and predictive-validity studies
remain necessary. Because fNIRS cannot feasibly be administered to every member of a large military population, a
two-tier pathway is proposed: brief population-level digital screening followed by targeted NPRO-8 MIL assessment.
Ethical safeguards addressing voluntariness, privacy, command access, purpose limitation, and protection from
unauthorized selection or disciplinary use are integral to the framework. NPRO-8 MIL is presented as a screening and
longitudinal monitoring approach, not a psychiatric diagnostic or autonomous fitness-for-duty instrument.

articles_hidden.title: GEST-A: A Hierarchical and Dynamic Framework of Conceptual Abstraction
articles_hidden.authors: Andriy Myachykov; Martin H Fischer
articles_hidden.abstract: Abstraction is central to human cognition, yet the term covers at least three senses that are routinely conflated: abstractness (how far a concept is removed from perceptible experience), specificity (how general or inclusive a category is), and the process by which conceptual change. We propose GEST-A (Grounded, Embodied, Situated Trajectories of Abstraction), a hierarchical and dynamic framework that separates these senses. Being abstract is a concept’s position in a dimensional space of grounding (physical-world constraints), embodiment (body-specific sensorimotor and interoceptive experience), and situatedness (dependence on context of use), with specificity as an orthogonal descriptor. Becoming abstract, in this view, is a trajectory through this space, driven by generalization and re-weighting of grounded, embodied, and situated content, and linked to a shift in feature structure from complete overlap to family resemblance. Using number concepts to illustrate these dynamics, we position GEST-A against earlier hybrid accounts of grounding, clarify that linguistic labels are cues and binding devices rather than constituting concepts, and argue that abstract concepts constrain rather than refute embodied cognition. We also revisit concreteness ratings and the symbol grounding problem and derive testable predictions. Abstract concepts reveal language as a powerful scaffold for building conceptual knowledge that exceeds individual sensorimotor experience.

articles_hidden.title: Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing Need a Better Definition of “Test”
articles_hidden.authors: Petr Palíšek
articles_hidden.abstract: Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing determine their scope by defining a “test”. This definition is of practical consequence due to the significance of Standards for test evaluation, individual-level and policy decisions, and legal proceedings. I argue the current version lacks sufficient clarity. In light of the ongoing revision of the Standards, I consider the language of the current codex and its purpose, along with its predecessors, and propose a new definition of “test” that addresses the issues of the current definition – big and small – while being rooted in the contemporary approach to test validity. The new definition helps clarify how Standards regulate different kinds of psychological and educational testing, including the anticipated rise in AI-driven assessment.

articles_hidden.title: The effectiveness of a therapeutically applied Dungeons and Dragons group intervention in a community mental health setting – Protocol for a randomised controlled trial.
articles_hidden.authors: Terry Rae; Matthew Modini; Poppy Watson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective 
The use of Therapeutically Applied Role-Playing Games (TA-RPGs) in mental health treatment settings has grown in popularity and early efficacy investigations appear promising. However, the use of TA-RPGs for the treatment of anxiety and depression has rarely been studied in people who present with comorbid complex mental health issues. While one recent waitlist-controlled trial has reported that a TA-RPG (Dungeons and Dragons with embedded CBT) reduced mental health symptomatology, this now needs to be replicated with a more robust experimental design. Publishing this protocol methodology before the study is completed aims to increase transparency and aid other researchers conducting similar research in this advancing field.  
Methods 
The authors propose a two-group randomised controlled trial testing the efficacy of a CBT-infused, therapeutically applied, 8-week Dungeons and Dragons group program. An active control group will play board games for a comparable amount of time. Participants will be consumers receiving care at a community mental health centre with complex care needs. Outcome measures for anxiety and depressive symptomatology will be collected before and after participation in both groups, with the intervention group also completing outcome measures at 12 months follow up. In this protocol paper the intervention will be outlined in detail. The trial is registered on the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry: ACTRN12625000296437.

articles_hidden.title: New money, no money, and psychological inheritance in the elasticity of 21st century happiness
articles_hidden.authors: Kai Ruggeri; Rafaella Osores Urday; Sofia Pelica; Sarah Ashcroft-Jones
articles_hidden.abstract: The role of financial resources in subjective well-being is extensively studied, yet with many unresolved debates on the precise association, inflection points, or applications. Using multidimensional data from 91 countries (N=53,589), we find near-universal support for a positive association, which is strongest in wealthier countries and, globally, highly elastic as household incomes surpass local costs of living. Uniquely, we observe a “psychological inheritance”, where the strongest associations are determined by economic class in childhood, even after significant upward mobility by adulthood. We also find inelasticity in well-being at the top and bottom of income distributions, which largely indicates satiation and decoupling at wealth extremes. Across countries, well-being surpasses average at household incomes around 4.5 times the cost of living. Downward mobility is linked with substantial declines but likewise better outcomes than those of equivalent adult incomes that started lower economically, suggesting a psychological endowment where starting point and relative stability are as vital as growth, though the association is strongest in wealthier countries. The link between income and well-being is therefore strongly supported while personal financial history and broader economic environment have substantial impacts on how money relates to happiness, and thus, to individual and population well-being.

articles_hidden.title: Longitudinal Associations Between Meta-Perceptions of Friends’ Reactions and Physical and Relational Aggression Perpetration During Early Adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Wyatt Thomas Brown; Erika Blair; Terri Sullivan
articles_hidden.abstract: Peer contexts can support or deter aggressive behavior perpetration in early adolescence. Relatively little is known, though, about how an individual’s expectations of their friends’ reactions to aggressive and non-aggressive behaviors inform physical and relational aggression perpetration. Participants (N = 527) were middle schoolers recruited from three schools in the Southeastern United States as part of a larger violence prevention program. Students completed self-report measures of meta-perceptions and recent relational and physical aggression perpetration at four timepoints across two academic years. We specified separate random intercept cross-lagged panel models for each subtype of aggression. We found evidence for stable between-person associations. Within-person fluctuations in meta-perceptions did not predict subsequent aggression perpetration, nor vice versa. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing individual differences from dynamic change processes in the study of aggressive behavior during early adolescence.
