articles_hidden.title: The Lyric Focus Questionnaire (LFQ):  Measuring Individual Differences in Song Listening
articles_hidden.authors: Dominique T Vuvan; Julia Cannistraro; Rachel Goodkind; Megha Sharda
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent years have seen a significant increase in the use of songs, which contain an integrated music/language signal, as experimental stimuli. This has created a need for standardized tools to measure individual differences in song perception. The current article reports the development of the Lyric Focus Questionnaire (LFQ), which measures the degree to which a song listener’s cognitive resources are oriented towards the lyrics versus the other musical features (i.e., pitch, rhythm, timbre). In Study 1, we used exploratory factor analysis to reduce 121 candidate items down to 12 items for the LFQ. In Study 2, we used confirmatory factor analysis and internal consistency measures to ascertain the unidimensional structure of the LFQ. In Studies 3 and 4, we demonstrated that the LFQ is correlated to comprehension of lyrics but not to the ability to exactly recall lyrics. In Study 5, we aggregated data from the first four studies to create initial norms for the Lyric Focus Questionnaire and to explore discriminant validity between Lyric Focus and musical and literary activities with more statistical power than in each study alone. The LFQ is presented as a practical, valid, and reliable tool for researchers interested in the relation between music and language.

articles_hidden.title: Overcoming the Empirical Challenges of Geometric Similarities: A Model-Based Review
articles_hidden.authors: Florian Ismael Seitz
articles_hidden.abstract: Similarity is fundamental to cognition, shaping both foundational and higher-order processes. Cognitive theories often adopt a geometric approach, where similarity is defined by the distance or angle between objects in a psychological space, successfully explaining many perceived similarity relations. However, the validity of such geometric similarity models has been questioned by diverse empirical challenges, such as violations of the metric axioms (minimality, symmetry, and triangle inequality), the common features effect (common features increasing similarity), contextual effects (similarity relations shifting with the presence of other objects), and nearest neighbor effects (single objects considered as most similar to many others). The present work reviews evidence showing that geometric similarity models can address many of these challenges through psychologically plausible extensions of the model formalizations. Some extensions add parameters within the standard framework, such as feature-specific attention or object-specific biases (e.g., salience or frequency). Others generalize the geometric framework itself, through similarity functions that go beyond distances or angles, or psychological spaces that represent objects as something other than points on a multidimensional map. Each extension addresses specific empirical challenges while maintaining cognitive plausibility. These findings suggest that geometric models, when appropriately extended, provide a robust foundation for understanding human similarity relations and offer a path toward comprehensive theories of higher-order cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Development and validation of a prognostic tool for antenatal depressive symptoms: Statistical analysis plan for a two-stage model integrating self-reported and biomarker measures
articles_hidden.authors: Ibrahim; Shahirose Sadrudin Premji; Shehzad Ali; Jaime Delgadillo
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Antenatal depression is common, under-detected, and harms mothers and infants. Pakistan has Asia’s highest perinatal depression prevalence and an estimated national economic burden of US$16.5 billion. About 9.7 million Pakistani women become pregnant each year, and roughly 3.6 million may experience antenatal depression. Routine detection relies on self-report scales (e.g., Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale [EPDS]); whether biomarkers add prognostic value is largely untested. 
Objective: Develop and validate a multivariable prognostic tool (MPT) to predict clinically significant depressive symptoms (EPDS ≥ 10) and assess the added value of biomarker data.
Methods: We will use secondary data (N = 1,621) from the Pakistani Pregnancy Cohort at the Aga Khan Hospital for Women and Children, Sindh. Self-reported predictors across eight domains (demographic, socioeconomic, behavioural, mental health, clinical history, pregnancy-related, and social network) plus biomarkers will inform MPT development. In Stage 1 we will compare supervised classifiers (regularized regression, decision trees, support vector machines, and neural networks) to logistic regression. Models will be trained with stratified five-fold cross-validation and nested L1 selection within folds to retain the smallest predictor set within 0.01 area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of the full mode. External cross-validation on an independent hold-out sample will report ROC-AUC, area under the precision-recall curve (relative to prevalence), calibration, sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values. Decision thresholds will be set on training data and applied unchanged. In Stage 2 we will build a biomarker-augmented model and compare it to the optimized self-report model using paired AUC tests and reclassification metrics; exploratory clustering will identify participant subgroups. Pre-specified criteria (ROC-AUC ≥ 0.70; calibration slope 0.8–1.2; sensitivity ≥ 0.70; positive net benefit) will determine progression to prospective validation studies in new samples. 
Expected Outcomes: A pragmatic self-report prognostic tool and evidence on whether biomarkers meaningfully improve prediction and justify added complexity.

articles_hidden.title: Characterizing the Association between Delinquency and Parenting Practices Across Adolescence: Longitudinal Associations and the Role of Genetic Liability
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah J Brislin; Maia Choi; Leigh Lustig; Holly E Poore; Sally I Kuo; Danielle Dick
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Parenting practices are a potential mechanism through which adolescent delinquent behavior can be modified. However, it remains unclear whether associations between parenting and delinquency reflect stable differences between families or dynamic processes unfolding within families over time. The current study disentangled the between- and within-person associations between delinquency and parenting across adolescence and whether genetic propensity toward externalizing, indexed by a polygenic score (EXT PGS), was associated with stable between-person differences in delinquency and parenting 

Methods: Participants were 2,184 adolescents assessed annually from ages 12 to 17 as part of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development- Social Development sub-study. Parents and youth reported on delinquency and parenting dimensions (corporal punishment, inconsistent discipline, poor monitoring, positive parenting). Random-intercept cross-lagged panel models separated between-person and within-person associations. We evaluated the association between the EXT PGS and the random intercepts. 
Results: Between-persons, adolescents with higher average delinquency experienced higher average levels of corporal punishment, inconsistent discipline, and poor monitoring and lower positive parenting. EXT PGS was associated with higher levels of delinquency and with higher corporal punishment, inconsistent discipline, and poor monitoring, as well as lower youth-reported positive parenting and accounted for approximately 4%–8% of variance shared between delinquency and parenting. Within-person, higher delinquency was associated with subsequent increases in youth-reported corporal punishment, but not parent-reported corporal punishment. Reciprocal associations emerged between delinquency and poor monitoring in both parent- and youth-report models and between delinquency and youth-reported inconsistent discipline. No longitudinal associations emerged between positive parenting and delinquency.
Conclusions: Associations between parenting and delinquency reflected both stable individual differences and dynamic developmental processes. The EXT PGS contributed to stable differences in delinquency and parenting, while longitudinal associations varied across parenting dimensions. These findings suggest that a focus on decreasing inconsistent discipline and increasing parental monitoring may be particularly relevant for mitigating delinquency.

articles_hidden.title: Current Topics in the Encephalographic Study of Visual Attention
articles_hidden.authors: Dock H Duncan; Kabir Arora; Samson Chota; Brandi Lee Drisdelle; Freek van Ede; Tobias Feldmann-Wüstefeld; Oscar Ferrante; Norman Forschack; Surya Gayet; Clayton Hickey
articles_hidden.abstract: An  enduring topic of scientific interest since the beginning of cognitive psychological research is visual attention. This phenomenon describes the process by which certain visual percepts are prioritized for deeper processing in the brain, while others receive reduced processing and thereby exert less influence on perception and behavior. In our daily lives, visual attention is critical to performance across countless situations—from navigating busy traffic to maintaining focus on a friend in a crowded room. Therefore, understanding the neural mechanisms that dictate how we select relevant visual information and filter out distractions is central to understanding one of the brain's most fundamental cognitive abilities. Because these attentional processes unravel rapidly in time and are reflected in dynamic patterns of cortical activity, encephalographic measures (i.e. electro- and magneto- encephalography) have been popular tools for their study. In 2025, attention researchers from across Europe gathered in Amsterdam for two days of meetings, discussion, and debate on current issues and future avenues in the encephalographic investigation of attention. This perspective piece distills the ideas and topics that emerged from that meeting into a field guide to contemporary encephalographic research on visual attention. It provides a snapshot of several active research areas in visual attention, highlights where they are heading, and which questions are likely to shape their future. We hope that this piece will be especially useful for early career researchers looking to enter the field but unsure about what their next research question should be.

articles_hidden.title: Polarity and the speed of scalar implicature processing
articles_hidden.authors: Michael Vrazitulis; J E Loy; Vera Demberg
articles_hidden.abstract: Scalar implicatures (SIs) such as the inference from 'some' to 'some but not all' are known to vary in processing cost. According to the Polarity Hypothesis (van Tiel et al., 2019; van Tiel & Pankratz, 2021), this cost depends on the polarity of the scalar term: SIs from positively polar expressions (e.g., 'some' implicating 'some but not all') are expected to be slower to compute than literal interpretations, while the reverse should hold for SIs from negatively polar expressions, sometimes referred to as indirect SIs (e.g., 'not all' implicating 'not all but some'). We tested this prediction in a sentence–picture verification experiment with 538 English-speaking participants. Each participant judged whether sentences containing weak or strong scalar terms matched a corresponding picture, allowing us to measure response times as an index of processing effort. Our results showed no clear evidence for the Polarity Hypothesis effect. Specifically, we found that the effect strongly varies across the different scales included in our experiment. We additionally conducted a meta-analysis pooling our estimate with all existing evidence so far: the pooled effect is small and in the predicted direction, but the study-specific estimates behind it vary widely in magnitude. Surprisingly, our results do also not clearly validate the traditional assumption of a B&N effect (Bott & Noveck, 2004), i.e., a general polarity-independent processing slowdown under SIs: a subsequent analysis including trial order revealed that the B&N effect was present in early trials of our study, whereas later trials do not show the effect. Overall, we conclude that polarity may influence the speed of scalar implicature processing, but that this effect is not robust across all types of scales.

articles_hidden.title: A partial least squares approach for within-subject correlations in neuroscience
articles_hidden.authors: Isaac Kinley; Reece Pierre Roberts; Donna Rose Addis
articles_hidden.abstract: Partial least squares correlation (PLSC) is a multivariate technique used in neuroscience to capture patterns of relationships between neural data and covariates of interest. Conventionally, PLSC captures between-subjects correlations (e.g., between average neural activation and average task performance). However, within-subject correlations (e.g., trial-by-trial relationships between neural activation and subjective ratings or stimulus attributes) are often of interest as well. Thus, we introduce an extension of PLSC to capture within-subject correlations. We validate this approach against related parametric methods and demonstrate that it detects known effects in simulated data and reproduces published findings in open fMRI and EEG datasets. This method is freely available as part of the pyplsc and mne-plsc Python packages.

articles_hidden.title: The Cognitive Structure of the WPPSI-IV: What Can Network Analysis Tell Us?
articles_hidden.authors: John Hite
articles_hidden.abstract: The Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence, Fourth Edition (WPPSI-IV), is widely used to assess young children’s cognitive abilities. Its indices describe performance in domains such as verbal comprehension and working memory, but evidence for interpreting these as distinct abilities remains limited. This study examined whether exploratory graph analysis (EGA), a network method, could recover the proposed index groupings from published normative correlations for ages 2:6 to 3:11 (n = 600) and 4:0 to 7:7 (n = 1,100). Simulations tested whether the same method could recover those groupings when separate, correlated factors generated the data. The main EGA procedure placed the primary subtests in one group. It also produced one group in 99.6% to 100% of samples generated from the index models, so it could not distinguish those models from simpler alternatives. In the older band, however, factor models fit better with several factors than with one. Recovery depended on factor correlations, the number of subtests per factor, and a built-in check for a single dimension. Groupings also changed with subtest coverage. For school psychologists, a one-group network result, however consistent, cannot by itself show whether WPPSI-IV index scores reflect distinct abilities.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond individual features: Identifying computational principles in perceiving visual beauty
articles_hidden.authors: Mustafa Alperen Ekinci; Philipp Flieger; Daniel Kaiser
articles_hidden.abstract: Prior research in empirical aesthetics has related beauty to visual features like curvature, color, or shape. Although these feature-based accounts have identified reliable visual correlates of beauty, the literature on feature preferences is highly fragmented, with individual features studied for individual stimulus domains. Here, we argue that making further progress hinges on complementing feature-based approaches with approaches aimed at distilling computational principles that underlie the perception of beauty. Recent advances in computational neuroscience can drive this new line of research by linking visual beauty to the coding of visual information in artificial neural networks and the biological brain. We highlight two examples of how this approach has identified overarching computational principles. First, metabolic processing costs, both in artificial and biological vision, are inversely related to perceived beauty, suggesting that beauty may reflect energy-efficient, fluent visual coding. Second, integrative processing in artificial and biological vision captures the efficient spatial representation of image elements across space and predicts beauty ratings. Synthesizing these findings, we derive a neuro-computational framework for assessing computational principles in the perception of beauty, which uses artificial neural networks for exploration at scale and then validates candidate principles using human behavior and brain data. We discuss candidate principles that could be explored using this approach, like spatiotemporal predictability, and delineate how the new insights could be reconciled with feature-based approaches. In conclusion, complementing feature-based studies with studies targeting computational principles promises a comprehensive and mechanistic understanding of why certain visual stimuli are perceived as beautiful, and others are not.

articles_hidden.title: Collider Bias in Partner Preference Research: A Methodological Extension of Eastwick et al. (2024)
articles_hidden.authors: Robin Lange
articles_hidden.abstract: Observational research on partner preference-matching commonly conditions on a sample of (most desired) partners. When examined through the lens of causal inference, this configuration constitutes conditioning on a collider variable. This thesis introduces and applies directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) as a framework for assessing corresponding collider bias within the large-scale cross-cultural dataset of Eastwick et al. (2024, N = 10,358, 43 countries). Building on this, a three-layer methodological framework is developed to distinguish three distinct sources of bias: confounding by measured background characteristics, intertrait confounding among the 35 attributes, and residual collider restriction bias arising from the sampling procedure itself. The trait-by-trait level metric of Eastwick et al. (2024) was replicated, followed by a hierarchical multivariate extension entering all 35 ideal preferences and partner attributes simultaneously across four nested models. Results show that demographic and individual-difference covariates contribute low aggregate variance (H1), that multivariate adjustment substantially attenuates both main effects and preference-matching interactions relative to the trait-by-trait approach (H2), and that idiosyncratic matching effects remain near zero even after full adjustment (H3). The discussion situates these findings within the broader context of the research design. Taken together, the methodological evaluation raises the question whether the original preference-matching hypothesis (H0) is adequately testable under the conditions of the present study design. The conclusion identifies the analysis of unselected peer targets as the most direct empirical path toward disentangling residual collider bias from genuine absence of idiosyncratic matching.

articles_hidden.title: Cross-Symptoms Interactions Fail to Predict Future Symptom States Across Four Ecological Momentary Assessment Datasets
articles_hidden.authors: Leema Hamid; Sílvia García-Hernández; Björn S. Siepe; Marius Gruber; Jonathan Repple; Andreas Reif; Manuel Brenner
articles_hidden.abstract: Symptom networks have emerged as a popular framework for characterizing the interactions among psychiatric symptoms. Estimated from longitudinal ecological momentary assessment (EMA) recordings, they promise individualized insights into psychopathology and its treatment. Yet whether these networks can be robustly estimated from the short, noisy, and irregularly sampled time series typical of EMA studies remains an open question. We address this through the lens of predictive validity: do estimated cross-symptom connections improve forecasts of future symptom states? In a systematic analysis spanning four public EMA datasets covering different symptoms and sampling schemes, we find that they largely do not. In 273 of 313 participants, symptom networks are outperformed by networks that only use every individual symptom's past to predict its future, indicating that estimated cross-symptom connections tend to worsen out-of-sample predictions rather than improve them. This pattern holds across estimation strategies from unregularized Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) to multilevel hierarchical modeling and nonlinear state-space models, suggesting that cross-symptom connections are difficult to identify given the characteristics of real EMA data. Simulation studies support this interpretation, showing that even when ground-truth data is generated by a network model mirroring realistic EMA conditions, cross-symptom structure is often not recovered with sufficient precision to yield a predictive advantage. These findings raise questions about the interpretive framework built on idiographic symptom networks, and suggest that progress may require either measurement designs that make cross-symptom influence more identifiable, or models with less ambitious inferential targets than the recovery of directed cross-symptom effects.

articles_hidden.title: Mental Time Travel is not Unique to Episodic Memory
articles_hidden.authors: Karl Szpunar; Öykü Ekinci; Sabrina Laurenne Valenzano; Mila Mac Neil; Cabildo Anne; Donna Rose Addis
articles_hidden.abstract: The subjective sense of mentally reliving the past is considered the key distinguishing feature of episodic memory—a neurocognitive system supporting recollection of specific life events. We present data from two pre-registered studies of musically-evoked autobiographical memory demonstrating that this subjective sense of mental reliving accompanies not just memories for specific events, but also more general autobiographical representations. Groups of 35- , 45- , and 55-year-old participants reported memories in response to musical cues that had been popular during their time in high-school, university, and early adulthood. Participants also rated the level of specificity and sense of mental time travel associated with each memory. Cumulative link mixed model analyses revealed that participants endorsed the presence of the subjective sense of mental time travel for specific, general, and lifetime period memories. Implication of reliving broader swaths of the personal past are discussed in relation to theories of episodic and autobiographical memory.

articles_hidden.title: Refining MLU-like metrics in parent-child speech: Measurement properties and decision aids for language-inclusive measures of speech complexity
articles_hidden.authors: Rui Qi Choo; Yi Han Victoria Chua; Fei Ting Woon; Annabel Loh; Shaza binte Amran; Vinitha Selvarajan; Sheetal Sahana Vimalraj; Wong Jin Yi; Suzy J Styles
articles_hidden.abstract:
Mean Length Utterance (MLU) has two problems: High analytic flexibility, and a lack of theoretical justification for data handling choices (e.g., selection of metrics; approach to multilingual speech). We evaluate multiple MLU-like metrics in a large corpus of child-directed speech from multilingual Singapore. Using an existing dataset of wordless picture-book sharing between parent-child dyads with frequent translanguaging (N = 146: English, Mandarin Chinese, Malay, Tamil), we compare metrics across the full sample, and common subsamples. 
Total speech, central tendency and extreme bounds of complexity all show significant developmental trajectories (p<.05), with larger effect sizes when larger subsamples are included in analysis. The metrics perform well when samples are maximally inclusive for languages spoken and types of speech. As some metrics performed better in certain contexts, we present a decision-tree as a reproducible, pre-registerable pathway for deciding which measurement of MLU-like syntactic complexity is best for data of different types.

articles_hidden.title: Large Eating Episodes, Cannabis Use, and Health in US Adults: A Cross-Sectional and Exploratory Mortality Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Elizabeth Webb Lampe; Kavish Chapra; Nicholas C. Jacobson
articles_hidden.abstract: Cannabis use is common and increases appetite, which may lead to large eating episodes that overlap with binge eating pathology. However, whether large eating episodes are related to health outcomes among individuals who use cannabis is not known. To address this gap, we analyzed seven cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES; 2005 to 2018) including 18,709 adults aged 20 to 59 years (2,578 current, 7,394 past, and 8,737 never cannabis users). A large eating episode was defined as an eating occasion of at least 1,500 kcal on either of two 24-hour dietary recalls. Among current cannabis users, survey-weighted logistic regression with Benjamini-Hochberg correction estimated adjusted associations between large eating episodes and 29 health outcomes. The weighted prevalence of a large eating episode was 30.3% among current cannabis users, 22.2% among past users, and 19.3% among never users. Among current users, a large eating episode was associated with higher odds of fair or poor self-rated health (adjusted odds ratio [OR] = 1.75, 95% CI [1.27, 2.41], p < .001, q = .022). No other association remained significant after correction, although nominal associations were observed for household food insecurity, obesity, abdominal obesity, and elevated glycated hemoglobin. Notably, adults with both current cannabis use and a large eating episode had higher odds of fair or poor health than each of the other three groups (ORs = 1.79 to 1.85, all p < .001). In exploratory analyses, the hazard of death was higher for adults with both exposures after adjustment for age and sex (hazard ratio [HR] = 2.08, 95% CI [1.31, 3.31]), though it did not remain significantly higher after full adjustment (HR = 1.40, 95% CI [0.88, 2.21]). Findings suggest that asking about eating patterns may help clinicians identify individuals who use cannabis and may be experiencing health-related distress. Longitudinal studies measuring loss of control over eating, cannabis frequency, and product type are critical for determining whether eating patterns affect health.

articles_hidden.title: Prevalence, Burden, and Disability Associated with Co-occurring Binge Eating Among U.S. Adults with Cannabis-Involved Drug Use Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Elizabeth Webb Lampe; Ya-Wen Chang; Nicholas C. Jacobson
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite established appetite-stimulating effects of cannabis use, binge eating is seldom assessed in these samples. Its prevalence, clinical importance, and demographic reach among people with cannabis-involved drug use disorder are largely unknown. We analyzed 12,591 adults from the Collaborative Psychiatric Epidemiology Surveys who completed the eating disorder and substance use modules. Using design-weighted estimation, we estimated prevalence of binge eating among adults with a cannabis-involved drug use disorder and examined whether binge eating marks greater burden and disability and whether it differs by demographic group. Recurrent binge eating affected 11.2% of adults with a cannabis-involved drug use disorder (95% CI [8.4, 14.7]). Separately, 5.5% met criteria for DSM-IV binge eating disorder. Prevalence rose across levels of cannabis involvement (adjusted OR per level = 2.11, 95% CI [1.75, 2.55]). Adults with both conditions had the highest prevalence of suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, major depression, and generalized anxiety disorder. At least one lifetime suicide attempt was reported by 27.8% of this group and by only 3.3% of adults with neither condition. Binge eating alone was associated with a level of functional disability comparable to cannabis-involved drug use disorder alone, while adults with both conditions had the highest WHODAS time out of role and role impairment scores. Among adults with cannabis-involved drug use disorder, binge eating also marked a more damaging drug course. Among adults with a cannabis-involved drug use disorder, recurrent binge eating was more prevalent among women (17.4%) than men (8.6%). Men nevertheless made up an estimated 54.1% of affected adults. Prevalence ranged from 9.7% to 12.3% across racial and ethnic groups. Findings indicate that binge eating is common and linked with adverse outcomes among those with cannabis-involved drug use disorder, thus warranting targeted interventions.

articles_hidden.title: How Asian American and Black American Adults Define Ethnicity, Race, and Nationality: A Qualitative Thematic Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Shujianing Li; Daniel James Sanji; Richard M. Lee; Sa-kiera Tiarra Jolynn Hudson
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on ethnicity, race, and nationality often conceptualizes and measures these identities independently, overlooking their interconnectedness. Perceptions of, and associations among, these identities could differ across racial groups, given distinct migration and racialization contexts in the U.S. Furthermore, nationality has not been thoroughly explored in ethnicity and race research. This study examined how individuals from groups with different migration and racialization histories (i.e., Asian and Black Americans) define ethnicity, race, and nationality. In a cross-sectional survey conducted on Prolific, 299 Asian American and 284 Black American adult participants reported their definitions of ethnicity, race, and nationality using open-ended responses. The definitions were thematically analyzed and reviewed between- and within-group variations. Definitions of ethnicity, race, and nationality shared similarities between samples: ethnicity by cultural components or family and ancestry; race by shared physical, genetic, and biological traits; and nationality by birthplace, belonging, and affiliation. Geographic locations also defined all three identities. However, Asian Americans commonly perceived ethnicity as narrower than race. Black Americans viewed the two identities as interchangeable and more frequently defined race as a social construct. Nationality had more ties to citizenship for Asian Americans than for Black Americans. Improved theorization and measurement of ethnic, racial, and national identity and the explicit inclusion of national contexts when discussing ethnic-racial identities are necessary.

articles_hidden.title: Neural correlates of dreaming during N2 sleep: Spatial and phenomenological characteristics
articles_hidden.authors: Vincent Rochas; Kevin Mammeri; Laurence Bayer; Giulio Tononi; Lampros Perogamvros
articles_hidden.abstract: Previous studies on the neural correlates of dreaming using high-density EEG (hdEEG) and the serial awakening paradigm have identified posterior brain regions related to dreaming, with maximal activity over occipital areas. Here, we first aimed to extend these findings by examining EEG activity associated with dreaming during N2 sleep in a larger sample and using improved analytical methods. Second, we investigated whether EEG activity was associated with continuous ratings of perceptual and thought-related experiences. We have applied hdEEG (256 electrodes) with source localization and the serial awakening paradigm in N2 sleep of 39 participants to study the neural activity during different time windows preceding each awakening. We found that having a conscious experience with recall (CE) compared to no experience (NE) is related to increased beta/gamma frequencies in a widely distributed part of the cortex, with peak T-values in posterior occipital-temporal regions in the longer time window (30 s), and in parietal regions in the shorter time window (20 s). Exploratory regression analyses revealed significant associations between EEG activity and thought-related experience, but not perceptual experience. These findings highlight the need to distinguish between the neural correlates of different dimensions of dream experience and to investigate their temporal characteristics and variations across sleep stages.

articles_hidden.title: Bringing developmental science closer to families: Caregivers’ and professionals’ perspectives on participation in early childhood research
articles_hidden.authors: Ana Maria Portugal; Eugénia Ribeiro; Marlene Sousa; Isabel Soares; Adriana Sampaio
articles_hidden.abstract:
Developmental research has historically underrepresented families experiencing psychosocial adversity, partly due to barriers posed by in-person laboratory paradigms. Online, webcam-based methods may support more inclusive research, but their design must be informed by the communities they seek to include.
Four focus groups were conducted with caregivers of young children (n = 10) and professionals from child protection, health, and education settings (n = 12), exploring barriers and facilitators to participation, and attitudes toward online data collection. Transcripts were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, with participant resonance checks.
Families expressed concerns about privacy and the use of children’s images, while professionals described hypervigilance towards authority among multi-challenged families. Developmental feedback and resources were valued over financial incentives, and online participation was viewed favourably, conditional on material and researcher support. Inclusive developmental science requires moving closer to families’ spaces and priorities, for instance by running studies in places families already use.

articles_hidden.title: Linking Error Estimation for Mean-Geometric Mean and Pairwise Haberman Linking Across Multiple Time Points in the 2PL Model
articles_hidden.authors: Oskar Engels; Oliver Lüdtke; Alexander Robitzsch
articles_hidden.abstract: Longitudinal assessments link test forms through common items. Under item parameter drift, linked ability means and standard deviations depend on the item selection, adding a linking error (LE) to the standard error (SE). Treating mean-geometric mean linking and pairwise Haberman linking across three time points in the two-parameter logistic model as M-estimators, this article derives closed-form LEs and sandwich estimators of LE, SE, and total error (TE). Sandwich and item jackknife LE estimators are bias-corrected for person sampling, including dependent samples. In a simulation study, SE-based intervals undercovered increasingly with sample size, bias-corrected jackknife TE intervals reached acceptable coverage almost everywhere, and sandwich-based intervals undercovered with few items. Longitudinal mathematics data illustrate the estimators, with the LE exceeding the SE.

articles_hidden.title: A Latent Profile Analysis of Undergraduates’ Motivational Strategy Use and Its Relations to Achievement and Well-being
articles_hidden.authors: Fanyi Zeng; Luise von Keyserlingk; Jacquelynne S Eccles; Jutta Heckhausen
articles_hidden.abstract: College students encounter academic hurdles such as failing exams or missing goals. The Motivational Theory of Life-Span Development outlines goal engagement, goal adjustment, and self-protection control strategies for regulating behavior after setbacks. We examined profiles of intended control strategy use after midterms in difficult courses, and their predictors and outcomes. We identified four student profiles: Low, Medium, High, and Engaged Strategy. Lower midterm performance predicted membership in the High and Engaged Strategy profiles. Engaged Strategy students (high goal engagement, low goal adjustment and self-protection) outperformed High Strategy students and, in most quarters, Medium Strategy students in final course grades. High Strategy students (high engagement, goal adjustment, and self-protection) had the lowest final course grades. Both High and Engaged Strategy students reported more positive feelings than others, but High Strategy students also reported more negative feelings than Low Strategy students. Findings suggest that focusing on goal engagement after a setback is more adaptive than combining it with goal adjustment and self-protection, and that students need support in identifying adaptive strategies.

articles_hidden.title: When AI becomes social: the promise and risks of AI companions for mental health – a social brain perspective
articles_hidden.authors: Benjamin Becker; Nan Qiu; Christian Montag
articles_hidden.abstract: AI companions are emerging as psychosocial technologies that may reshape social connection and mental health, while also creating risks of emotional dependence. Here, we propose a social-brain framework explaining how attachment, reward, and emotion regulation systems may shape human–AI bonding. This framework highlights the importance of understanding how AI companionship may reshape social connection and mental health, suggests an overarching model that accounts for the complex interplay between the human interface, technology design and context, and provides insights for the responsible design of future AI systems.

articles_hidden.title: Adaptive auditory stimulation sustains auditory-respiratory coordination and promotes slowing of spontaneous breathing
articles_hidden.authors: Bavo Van Kerrebroeck; Pieter-Jan Maes; Ilse Van Diest
articles_hidden.abstract: Auditory feedback may influence breathing without explicit instructions to regulate it, but its precise impact remains unclear. We examined responses to adaptive and nonadaptive breath-like sounds during passive listening. Thirty-nine young adults completed four counterbalanced conditions: nonrhythmic filtered noise (Static), rhythmic sounds progressively slowing or speeding relative to initial breathing rate (Slowing and Speeding respectively), and sound adapting continuously to respiratory frequency and phase with a prescribed phase delay relative to respiration (Adaptive). Each condition included 4 min of nominal silence followed by 4 min of stimulation. Primary outcomes were breathing rate slopes, auditory–respiratory phase locking as a measure of auditory-respiratory coordination, respiratory sinus arrhythmia, and subjective relaxation. Breathing-rate trajectories differed across conditions; Adaptive showed a more negative slope than Static, although average rates were similar. Phase locking was higher and more sustained during Adaptive than during the nonadaptive rhythmic conditions. Respiratory sinus arrhythmia trajectories differed, but planned contrasts did not survive multiplicity correction. A relaxation composite score did not differ by condition, but an item-level analysis indicated less physical relaxation after Adaptive than Static. Secondary outcomes provided no evidence of increased cardiorespiratory coupling or reduced upper-trapezius muscle activity. Interestingly, the negative breathing-rate trajectories remained significantly different in Adaptive compared to Static after retaining only the 25 respondents that did not notice the sound’s adaptation to their breathing. These findings support adaptive auditory stimulation as a means of supporting auditory-respiratory coordination during uninstructed listening, with a modest and relative change in breathing rate. Clinical benefits and independence from intentional breathing control remain to be tested.

articles_hidden.title: Trust in AI: A Decision-Theoretic framework for Human–AI Interactions in the Digital Society
articles_hidden.authors: Leendert van Maanen; Martijn Mulder; Baptist Liefooghe
articles_hidden.abstract: Trust in artificial intelligence (AI) is crucial for ensuring productive human–AI interactions across domains ranging from medicine to finance. As AI systems become central in the digital society, understanding how people decide when to rely on algorithmic advice becomes increasingly important. This paper proposes that a decision-theoretic perspective is needed to explain how well-calibrated trust in AI can be achieved. We conceptualize trust in AI as a decision to delegate control to an artificial agent, balancing potential rewards and risks of following AI advice versus relying on one’s own judgment. Framed this way, established decision-making theories such as Prospect Theory, Evidence Accumulation Models, and Reinforcement Learning offer valuable insights into the cognitive processes that underlie trust in AI. These theories offer formal, computational models to explain how individuals evaluate AI-generated advice, weigh risks and rewards, form biases, and update trust based on feedback, enabling precise hypotheses about when and why people accept or reject AI advice. By grounding trust in cognitive theory, we offer a roadmap for empirical research that moves beyond surface-level behaviors and toward mechanistic understanding. We conclude that a decision-theoretic approach can enhance psychological insight and guide the responsible design of AI systems within the digital society that are better aligned with human cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Unequal burdens of research in underrepresented contexts: Developing language metrics and morphemising protocols for use in complex multilingual environments
articles_hidden.authors: Rui Qi Choo; Suzy J Styles; Yi Han Victoria Chua; Seraphina Fong; Vinitha Selvarajan; Sheetal Sahana Vimalraj; Annabel Loh; Shaza binte Amran; Wong Jin Yi; Fei Ting Woon
articles_hidden.abstract: In child language research and clinical speech language pathology settings, transcripts of speech are often used for investigations into language acquisition and development. The existing literature is heavily biased towards monolingual contexts, particularly from a small number of languages, meaning that there are few examples of theory-driven protocols for handling speech and deriving developmental metrics from contexts where multiple typologically diverse languages appear together. In the current report, we address limitations of existing approaches and describe a theory-driven protocol for transcription and morphemizing of multilingual translanguaged speech, as applied to large corpus of parent-child speech from multilingual Singapore. The protocol aims to be language-model neutral, treating all speech as valid input to the child, without excluding or separating by official language labels, and may be applicable to a variety of linguistic contexts. One key finding arising from this research was that applying the protocol created unique research challenges for the typological distinct languages used by parents in the local context (predominantly English, Mandarin Chinese, Malay and Tamil alongside unique lexical items from the local context, known as Red-Dot words), and that structural inequalities make those challenges more difficult to resolve for minoritized and under-resourced languages.

articles_hidden.title: Early-life adversity, childhood loneliness, and young adulthood educational achievement: a prospective study
articles_hidden.authors: Laura Cachón-Alonso; Sari Mullola; Jeanne Brooks-Gunn; Christian Hakulinen; Kaisla Komulainen; Marko Elovainio
articles_hidden.abstract: We examine (1) whether indicators of early-life adversity are associated with children’s loneliness complaints and their recurrence at ages 5 and 9; and (2) whether children’s loneliness complaints are associated with poorer educational achievement measured at age 22 after adjusting for early-life adversity indicators. We used data from the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study (US, original sample n=4,898; study sample n=2,456). Children’s loneliness complaints were reported by the principal caregiver. We applied (1) binomial logistic regression and (2) weighted g-computation. In our sample, 6.8% of children had recurrent caregiver-reported loneliness complaints. Indicators of socioenvironmental early-life adversity were associated with higher odds of loneliness complaints. Moreover, higher material hardship and lower neighborhood collective efficacy were associated with higher odds of complaints recurring at ages 5 and 9. We observed no association between caregiver-reported loneliness in childhood and later educational achievement. We note limitations in our measurement of childhood loneliness.

articles_hidden.title: A Cross-Cultural Comparison of the Attractiveness Halo Effect in Men and Women
articles_hidden.authors: Tobias L. Kordsmeyer; Letizia von Dewitz; Yaren Kirma; Sabine Ostermann; Julia Stern; Jean Carlos Natividade; Jaroslava Varella Valentova; Marco Antonio Correa Varella; Lars Penke
articles_hidden.abstract: According to the attractiveness halo effect, global person perceptions are biased by physical attractiveness: More attractive people are ascribed positive attributes like competence, prosociality, and health, with cross-cultural variation in such perceptions. However, extant cross-cultural studies mostly considered cross-cultural differences only in either observers or targets. This preregistered study explored cross-cultural nuances in the attractiveness halo effect for Brazilian and German target men and women, as perceived by Brazilian and German observers. Facial photos of 583 targets were judged separately for attractiveness, prosociality, health, intelligence, social competence, familiarity, and physical and social dominance by 554 Brazilian and 326 German observers. Ratings between Brazilian and German observers for the same target group and attribute were strongly positively correlated, except for familiarity for German male targets. Attractiveness halo effects were overall strong (stronger for health, social competence, and familiarity compared to social dominance, prosociality, and intelligence) and mostly consistent for Brazilian and German targets and observers, with few exceptions. Only for physical dominance, associations were mixed by target gender and nationality. This study supports a putative universality of attractiveness halo effects and also contributes to a deeper understanding of subtle variations in the halo effects of men’s and women’s attractiveness in more individualistic versus more collectivistic cultures.

articles_hidden.title: Visual Properties of E-Mobility Devices Shape Their On-Road Vulnerability: Effects of Size and Speed
articles_hidden.authors: Laura Wang; Madeline Jarvis; Ella Du Plessis; Ariella Stephen; Blake Jones; Narelle Haworth; Hinze Hogendoorn
articles_hidden.abstract: The brief visual window—often only hundreds of milliseconds—in which drivers predict the arrival of oncoming vehicles and decide whether to give way is critical for safe and efficient manoeuvring. E-mobility devices (EMDs) are a relatively new form of transportation and may challenge these decisions due to their small visual profile and relatively high operating speeds. Here, we examined whether observers show systematic biases when judging EMDs relative to other common vehicles, potentially contributing to their vulnerability in intersection crashes. Using naturalistic video stimuli spanning seven vehicle categories, we tested whether observers would overestimate the time-to-arrival (TTA) of EMDs and, consequently, accept smaller gaps for them to pass through an intersection. Consistent with this prediction, EMDs elicited greater biases in both TTA and gap judgements (N = 31 and N = 59), with these effects further amplified on a visually complex road. By comparing across vehicle categories under naturalistic viewing conditions, the results provide evidence that the amplified biases observed for EMDs arise from differences in the underlying visual signals available to observers—specifically, their smaller retinal size and potentially less reliable motion cues at higher speeds. Importantly, these biases were not explained by speed misperception: in a separate two-alternative forced-choice task (N = 49), EMDs were perceived as faster, not slower, than other vehicles at matched speeds. This dissociation indicates that TTA overestimation cannot be attributed to speed underestimation alone. Together, these findings link controlled psychophysical processes to real-world traffic behaviour, with implications for future experimental design and traffic safety policy.

articles_hidden.title: Do Meditators Stress Less? Long-Term Meditators Differ in Affective but Not Autonomic Responses to an Acute Psychosocial Stressor
articles_hidden.authors: Ivana Buric; George M. Slavich; Katarina Jaukovic; Gorkem Atilla; Tom Smeets
articles_hidden.abstract: Although regular meditation practice is widely assumed to buffer responses to stress, direct evidence from long-term meditators remains limited. We compared 80 long-term mindfulness meditators and 68 meditation-naïve controls on affective and autonomic responses to an acute psychosocial stressor, a modified Trier Social Stress Test (TSST). Negative and positive affect were assessed before and after the TSST, and vagally mediated heart rate variability (HRV) was assessed across baseline, stress anticipation, and recovery in a subsample of 70 participants. In preregistered analyses, meditators reported lower post-stress negative affect (ηp2 = .05) and higher post-stress positive affect (ηp2 = .04) than controls after accounting for pre-stress affect, age, and gender. Meditators’ lower emotion-regulation difficulties accounted for their lower negative and higher positive affect before the stressor but not for group differences in affective change. In contrast, meditators and controls did not differ in HRV, either overall or across TSST phases, with Bayesian analyses providing strong to extreme evidence for the absence of group effects (BF01 > 14). In exploratory analyses, meditators reported fewer and less severe stressors over the past year despite comparable lifetime stressor exposure. Long-term meditation was thus associated with modestly more favourable affective, but not autonomic, responses to an acute psychosocial stressor. The stress-buffering benefits associated with long-term meditation may therefore operate less through attenuated reactivity to acute stressors and more through processes that reduce stressor exposure or facilitate recovery in daily life.

articles_hidden.title: Etude comparative des répercussions émotionnelles chez les primo-intervenants (pompiers, SMUR) et les psychologues
articles_hidden.authors: Violette BARBIER-SORBA; Adolphe Béquet
articles_hidden.abstract:
Cette étude s'intéresse aux répercussions émotionnelles liées à la temporalité d’intervention chez deux catégories de professionnels exposées à une forte charge émotionnelle : les primo- intervenants (sapeurs-pompiers, membres du SMUR) et les psychologues, dits « intervenants différés ». L’objectif est de comparer les effets émotionnels selon que l’intervention ait lieu de manière immédiate ou différée. Une étude quantitative a été réalisée auprès de 286 participants âgés de 19 à 67 ans, exerçant comme pompiers, membres du SMUR ou psychologues depuis au moins un an. Ils ont répondu à trois questionnaires : le Work-Related Quality of Life (Van Laar et al., 2007), le Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (Watson et al., 1988), et un questionnaire socio-démographique. Les résultats ont permis de montrer qu’aucune différence significative n’a été observée entre primo-intervenants et psychologues concernant les émotions ressenties. En revanche, la qualité de vie au travail est plus élevée chez les psychologues et corrélée à des émotions plus positives. Les analyses statistiques montrent que la qualité de vie et la temporalité d’intervention sont deux prédicteurs significatifs des répercussions émotionnelles, bien qu’insuffisants à les expliquer entièrement. L’analyse lexicale complète ces résultats en mettant en évidence les stratégies de régulation adoptées par les professionnels.
Mots clés : Primo-intervenants, psychologues, traumatisme secondaire, impact émotionnel, qualité de vie au travail

This study focuses on the emotional repercussions related to the timing of intervention among two categories of professionals exposed to high emotional demands: first responders (firefighters, emergency medical service members) and psychologists, referred to as “delayed responders”. The aim is to compare emotional effects depending on whether the intervention occurs immediately or at a later time. A quantitative study was conducted with 286 participants aged 19 to 67, working as firefighters, EMS members, or psychologists for at least one year. They completed three scales : the Work-Related Quality of Life (Van Laar et al., 2007), the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (Watson et al., 1988), and a socio-demographic questionnaire. The results showed no significant difference between first responders and psychologists in terms of the emotions experienced. However, psychologists reported a higher quality of work life, which was associated with more positive emotions. Statistical analyses indicate that quality of life and intervention timing are two significant predictors of emotional repercussions, though not sufficient to fully explain them. Lexical analysis complements these findings by highlighting the regulation strategies adopted by professionals.
Keywords: First responders, psychologists, secondary trauma, emotional impact, work-related quality of life.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of finding and savoring kawaii aspects of animal pictures on affective ratings, mood, and prosocial behavior
articles_hidden.authors: Nonoka Nakamura; Hiroshi Nittono
articles_hidden.abstract: The Japanese word ‘kawaii’ describes not only an object’s cute attributes but also a positive feeling toward it. Although viewing cute objects can improve mood and encourage prosocial behavior, it remains unclear whether intentionally focusing on kawaii feelings enhances these effects. In two online experiments, participants viewed pictures of dogs and cats (N = 282) and other animals (N = 435). They were instructed to either find and savor the kawaii aspects of the animals or to find and describe their objective characteristics. The results showed that the picture ratings of valence, arousal, approach motivation, and kawaii were higher in the kawaii condition than in the objective condition. However, no significant differences were found between the conditions in terms of mood change or donation-related voluntary actions. Focusing on kawaii aspects can improve affective evaluation, but a one-time savoring session may not be sufficient to alter mood or behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Borderline personality disorder, a diagnosis that cannot be challenged: If rejecting the diagnosis is a symptom, can the diagnosis ever be wrong? A response to Chazhoor and Younger (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Laurence Cobbaert
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Chazhoor and Younger describe borderline personality disorder (BPD) as a diagnostic and management challenge in regional inpatient psychiatry, including patients' reluctance to accept the diagnosis and preference for autism, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or complex post-traumatic stress disorder (CPTSD). This Perspective examines the epistemic assumptions embedded in that framing and their implications for trauma, neurodivergence, gender diversity, sensory distress and iatrogenic harm.
Conclusions: Diagnostic disagreement is not evidence for the diagnosis being disputed. BPD is itself historically and culturally situated, and its application can relocate traumatic, neurodevelopmental, sensory and minority-stress-related distress into a purportedly disordered personality. When dissent, self advocacy or reports of harm are reinterpreted through the same construct, diagnostic reasoning risks becoming recursive and unfalsifiable. I argue for moving beyond BPD towards trauma-informed, neurodiversity-affirming, sensory-informed and epistemically just formulations that remain open to revision.

articles_hidden.title: Attention in model-based cognitive neuroscience: Mechanisms for optimization under constraint
articles_hidden.authors: Emily Ruth Weichart; Ryan Pierce Kirkpatrick; Jared Vance
articles_hidden.abstract: Two major criticisms of attention research are: 1) verbal theories lack the specificity to make falsifiable predictions about how the various mechanisms of attention operate; and 2) the term ``attention’’ is frequently ascribed to conceptually similar phenomena despite dissociable neural underpinnings. The field of model-based cognitive neuroscience is well-positioned to address (1) through mathematical formalization of hypothesized processes, but may perpetuate (2) insofar as similar algorithms and parameters may recur across modeling traditions without necessarily drawing upon a shared neuro-mechanistic basis. This review provides a function-first organization of the algorithms that have been hypothesized to implement or give rise to ``attention'' at various levels of processing: perception, decision-making, and learning. We ground mathematically-formalized processes in the performance-relevant objectives they serve and the processing constraints that limit them. In doing so, we provide a road map of the broader computational-level solutions that ``attention'' mechanisms have been invoked to provide.

articles_hidden.title: Development and Validation of the Mental Health Screening Tool for Children and Adolescents (MHST-CA)
articles_hidden.authors: Diana Vasile; Șerban Andrei Zanfirescu; Ana Cosmoiu; Teodora Georgescu; Marina Badea; Monica Senchiu; Dragos Iliescu; Alina Aldea
articles_hidden.abstract: Existing adolescent mental health screening instruments are predominantly symptom-focused, lack integration of biological, psychological, and social dimensions, and have limited validation evidence in Eastern European populations. This study describes the development and validation of the Mental Health Screening Tool for Children and Adolescents (MHST-CA), a brief self-report instrument grounded in the biopsychosocial model. Item generation drew on 22 focus groups (N > 200) and interviews with 31 specialists. An initial 132-item pool was reduced through exploratory factor analysis in a pilot sample (N = 237, ages 10-20) and confirmatory factor analysis in a validation sample (N = 496, ages 10-20, 58.1% female). For the final 27 items, the hypothesized correlated three-factor model was not supported (CFI = .88), whereas a bifactor model with a general factor and three biopsychosocial facets fit well (CFI = .92, TLI = .91, RMSEA = .06, SRMR = .05, ωH = .88, ECV = .76) and is proposed post hoc as the measurement model. Internal consistency was high (α = .84-.94) and measurement invariance held across gender and age group. The total score correlated with the DASS-Y (r = .82), CPSS (r = .73) and WEMWBS (r = -.69) and identified elevated posttraumatic stress symptoms (AUC = .90). Controlling for age, gender and the DASS-Y, the Biological and Social subscales added ΔR² = .085 in predicting well-being. The MHST-CA offers a brief, culturally grounded screening tool for Romanian adolescents, best interpreted as a total score. Limitations include reliance on self-report and a geographically restricted sample.

articles_hidden.title: Similarity Judgments Reveal the Multidimensional Representations of Naturalistic Faces
articles_hidden.authors: Natalie Peluso; Amanda K Robinson; Tijl Grootswagers; Julie Henry; Jessica Taubert
articles_hidden.abstract: The human face affords a remarkable array of complex social cues, yet our understanding of how it is spontaneously perceived relies almost exclusively on controlled, posed stimuli that suppress the natural variation which makes faces so informative. Here, using a data-driven similarity task with 75 naturalistic face images, we mapped 182,500 perceptual judgments across 365 adults aged 20 to 76. The results indicated that naturalistic face space was hierarchically organized by expressive and demographic cues: smiling faces formed a coherent category that transcended gender and age, whereas non-smiling adult faces stratified along apparent gender. Representational similarity analysis showed that affective dimensions (valence, intensity, energy), emotion category, demographic cues (age and gender), and image-based color each uniquely predicted similarity judgments, while specific personality traits and facial action unit intensity did not. These results demonstrate that highly variable naturalistic faces carry potent combinations of both categorical and dimensional information, advancing a more ecologically valid framework for understanding real-world social perception.

articles_hidden.title: The Power of Narrow Traits (PNT) Framework: How Behavior Accumulates Across Situations into Life Outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Michael P. Grosz
articles_hidden.abstract: Broad traits predict consequential life outcomes but are ill-suited to causal inference, whereas single narrow, behaviorally measured traits are more interpretable causally but predict weakly. The space of narrow traits is also so large that choosing among them is challenging. I propose the Power of Narrow Traits (PNT) framework to address both challenges. In a specific person, the causal effect of a narrow trait (e.g., talkativeness) on a specific outcome (e.g., social capital) accumulates across the situations in which the trait can be expressed as a state (e.g., talking) and in which that state influences the outcome, with situations described by their features. In its basic form, four factors multiply at each point of the feature space: (a) how often per year the person encounters such situations, (b) over how many years, (c) how strongly the trait translates into the state there, and (d) how strongly that state causally affects the outcome. These contributions are then summed over the situations the person encounters. The decomposition clarifies when narrow traits should be consequential, which traits to measure for a given outcome, why the same trait level leads to an outcome for some people but not for others, and how interventions can be tailored to each person's trait and situational profile. I formalize the framework, illustrate it with worked examples, relate it to existing theories, and derive six empirical predictions. PNT thus provides a unifying structure for future work on stable individual differences and life outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: llmClassificR: Text Classification with Large Language Models, Network Psychometrics, and Calibrated Uncertainty in R
articles_hidden.authors: Hudson Golino
articles_hidden.abstract: Text classification has become a central measurement problem in psychology and the social sciences, and the arrival of large language models (LLMs) multiplied the number of available strategies, from contextual encoders and embedding services to prompted generative models and, more recently, general-purpose classification models such as Jev, which return probabilities for typed questions about a text. The present paper introduces the R package llmClassificR, which brings these strategies together in a single, consistent interface, and shows how they can be combined with network psychometrics, complexity science, and modern uncertainty quantification. The package implements (a) unsupervised classification of texts with exploratory graph analysis applied to the embeddings of local encoder models, decoder LLMs, and embedding APIs, including a prime-weight encoding that combines the networks estimated from every transformer layer into a single multiplex representation; (b) supervised classification heads on frozen embeddings, evaluated by cross-validation; (c) prompted classification with generative LLMs, with shuffled batching, label validation, strict JSON Schema outputs, ensembles, and self-consistency; (d) retrieval-augmented, automated, and human-guided topic discovery; (e) Jev-based classification with Choice, Noul, and Score questions; (f) do-it-yourself Jev-like classifiers built from label descriptions and local or API embeddings; and (g) calibration, temperature scaling, Platt scaling, selective classification, and conformal prediction sets. The tutorial uses synthetic texts generated by LLMs, descriptions of emotional situations labeled by the people who wrote them (EmpatheticDialogues), and Reddit comments labeled by several raters (GoEmotions), which makes it possible to show how methods that look nearly perfect on synthetic data behave on real text, how the reliability of the labels limits the accuracy that any classifier can demonstrate, and how model uncertainty relates to human disagreement.

articles_hidden.title: Phantom limb behaviour and gaze during obstacle avoidance: obstacle shunning and tolerance after upper-limb amputation
articles_hidden.authors: David Crevillén Hernández; Manfredo Atzori; Steffi Weidt; Emily S. Cross; Gianluca Saetta
articles_hidden.abstract:
Phantom limb sensations persist in most amputees and offer a window into how the body is represented without sensory input from the missing limb. In this state, vision may help resolve conflicts between the perceived body and the physical world. In obstacle tolerance (OBT), the phantom remains present despite overlapping with physical matter; in obstacle shunning (OBS), it retracts or disappears. Whether these experiences extend beyond subjective perception to visual attention during action remains unclear.
We tested whether OBS and OBT are associated with distinct gaze and task-performance patterns during obstacle avoidance. Fifteen individuals with transradial amputation (7 OBS, 8 OBT) and 29 able-bodied controls physically executed or imagined a limb repositioning movement while avoiding an obstacle. We recorded gaze using mobile eye-tracking and quantified obstacle-directed dwell time using automated obstacle segmentation and fixation detection. We analysed trial duration and attention shifts between the obstacle and the limb or environment.
Bayesian mixed-effects models showed that participants with OBT spent less time looking at the obstacle when using the affected rather than the intact limb during motor execution. They were also more likely to make three or fewer attention shifts with the affected-limb, suggesting reduced obstacle monitoring when phantom–object overlap is tolerated. Participants with OBS took longer than controls during both motor execution and motor imagery.
These findings suggest that OBS and OBT are associated with distinct action-related visuospatial strategies. Phantom–object relations appear to extend beyond subjective experience to the visual and temporal organisation of behaviour around physical objects.

articles_hidden.title: Bonobos and chimpanzees: revisiting the aggression dichotomy
articles_hidden.authors: Ulrich Maloueki; Bekeli Nseu Mbomba
articles_hidden.abstract: Aggression in the genus Pan (including bonobos and chimpanzees) remains a central puzzle in primatology and anthropology. Traditionally framed as a dichotomy between “peaceful bonobos” and “violent chimpanzees,” recent findings challenge this view by documenting coalitionary aggression, maternal cannibalism, and lethal intergroup encounters in bonobos, alongside evidence that captive chimpanzees and bonobos exhibit comparable aggression levels. These observations highlight the importance of ecological context, demographic composition, and behavioral plasticity in shaping aggression. We propose that species identity is a weaker predictor of aggression in Pan than socioecological, demographic, social, and neuroendocrine context. While captivity offers methodological control, it also introduces confounds such as reduced group size, absence of fission–fusion dynamics, and enforced proximity. Conversely, wild studies reveal the ecological pressures, territorial defense, resource distribution, and interspecies competition that drive variation in aggression. Future research must integrate captive and free‑ranging data through hybrid protocols, quantify ecological and demographic drivers, and explore neuroendocrine mechanisms underlying sex‑specific aggression. An integrative review on Pan aggression will refine our understanding of adaptive strategies, illuminate the evolutionary roots of human social conflict, and advance comparative models of primate behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Testing Group Differences in Network Models using Bayesian Model Selection: A Tutorial
articles_hidden.authors: Jonas M B Haslbeck; Mona Klau; Tessa F. Blanken; Maarten Marsman
articles_hidden.abstract: Network models are increasingly used to model multivariate data and many research questions are about whether networks differ across groups. This tutorial provides an accessible introduction to Bayesian model-selection for testing group differences in networks, as implemented in the R package bgms. This approach provides posterior inclusion probabilities and Bayes factors for each group difference, allowing researchers to distinguish evidence for a difference from evidence for equality. We focus the tutorial on group differences in ordinal network models, since the vast majority of data in cross-sectional research are measured on ordinal scales. We explain the model parameters, prior choices, missing-data handling, convergence checks, checks of model fit, and the interpretation of posterior summaries of group differences. The workflow is illustrated with a reproducible comparison of problematic pornography use symptom networks in women and men.

articles_hidden.title: Reinforcement learning processes underlying the onset and maintenance of compulsive ritualistic behavior
articles_hidden.authors: No authors listed
articles_hidden.abstract: Compulsive rituals in OCD present a fundamental puzzle for theories of human learning. How can an action acquire value as a means of preventing harm even though the individual recognizes that the action has little or no causal influence on the feared outcome? We propose that this apparent contradiction can arise from automatic credit assignment, whereby actions that precede favorable outcomes are reinforced even when those actions are known to be causally irrelevant. When harm is anticipated but no adverse outcome occurs, the absence of harm may reinforce the preceding action, allowing an objectively ineffective behavior to acquire harm prevention value. We formalize this account using an actor-critic reinforcement learning model in which actions are performed under fluctuating states of subjective perceived threat. Simulations show that agents possessing such false credit assignment mechanisms develop persistent ritualistic behavior in an objectively uncontrollable environment. We find that ritualistic behavior is especially likely to persist when feared outcomes are rare and highly aversive, making the ritual appear consistently effective in preventing a catastrophe. We further describe the cost-effectiveness of ritualistic behavior, and provide a computational account of how compulsive rituals can emerge as goal-directed attempts to prevent harm, persist despite explicit causal knowledge, and subsequently acquire anxiety-reducing properties. This work may help explain the persistence of compulsive behavior and inform mechanisms through which therapy can reduce it.
